The Yoshida faimly grew immensely powerful later. === Formation of Yoshida Shinto === {{Main|Yoshida Shintō}} [[File:吉田兼倶肖像画.jpg|thumb|Yoshida Kanetomo]] During the {{ill|Ōnin|en}} reign, the {{ill|Ōnin War|en}} broke out and Kyoto was burnt to the ground, affecting many temples and shrines, and causing the abortion of imperial court rituals such as the Ōnin Festival and the coronation ceremony. One of the priests who was shocked by the upheaval was {{ill|Yoshida Kanetomo|en}}. Kanetomo, who was so upset that he lost his own {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}} to the war, as well as more than a dozen residents of the area around the shrine.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=182}} However, the loss of many ancient manuscripts due to the war led to the formation of a new Shinto theory called {{ill|Yoshida Shintō|en}}.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=234}} The {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Yoshida family|ja|吉田家}}, whose surname is {{ill|Radical 25|lt=Turabu|en|}}, was a family that specialized in Ketu (divination) in the Ministry of Divine Worship and succeeded to the position of Deputy Minister of Divine Worship for many generations. In the Middle Ages, {{ill|Urabe Kanekata|ja|卜部兼方}} became well versed in the study of the Chronicles of Japan, writing {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|en}}, and was called the "House of the Chronicles of Japan.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=181}}{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9861|access-date=2024-03-25|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} Kanetsu wrote "Shinto Taioi" and "Onna Shinto Meibyo Shu" to compile medieval Shinto thought, while incorporating discourses from various religions to present a new Shinto theory called "Yoshida Shinto". In the book, he classified Shinto into three categories: "Honjaku Enki Shinto" (auspicious signs handed down from shrine to shrine), "Ryobu Nariai Shinto", and "Motomune Sougen Shinto". He stated that the "Motomune Sougen Shinto" handed down by his family was the legitimate Shinto since the dawn of Japan, and defined God as "the spiritual head of heaven, earth and all things" and the Way as "the origin of all things and all actions".{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=236-237}} With regard to the relationship between Shinto, {{ill|Confucianism|en}} and {{ill|Buddhism|en}}, he strongly advocated the theory that Shinto was the root, [[Confucianism]] emerged as a branch and leaf in [[China]], and [[Buddhism]] blossomed as a fruit in [[India]].{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=113}} [[File:Yoshida_shrine_funeral_hall.jpg|left|thumb|{{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}} in {{ill|Sakyō-ku, Kyoto|lt=Sakyo-ku|en}} {{ill|Kyoto|Kyoto City|en}}]] He argued that Shinto has three aspects: "body," which is the essence, "aspect," which is the manifestation, and "use," which is the action, and that these actions govern all phenomena such as the sun and moon, cold and heat, and nature. In the end, Kaneku's theory of Shinto was a kind of pantheism in which God exists within all beings, and God is omnipresent throughout the universe.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=237-238}} Kaneku formed many rituals along with his Shinto theories. First, he established the Omotoshae Shrine in the precincts of {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}}, which he proclaimed to be the place of worship for the Inner Shrine, Outer Shrine, eight temples, and more than 3,000 Shinto shrines, the root of Shinto rituals in Japan since the time of Jimmu, and the main shrine of all Shinto shrines in Japan.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=235-236}} In addition, under the influence of esoteric Buddhism, he invented the {{ill|Homa (ritual)|lt=Homa|en}} event, in which a fire is kindled in an octagonal platform with a furnace at its center, and grain and porridge are thrown into the fire while praying, forming the San-dan event along with the 18 Shinto events and Sougen Shinto events.{{Cite web |title=吉田神道行事壇 |url=http://museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/exhibition/detail/id=4 |access-date=2021-03-02 |publisher=國學院大學博物館}} These teachings were expounded by the "Three Nerves" of the Tengen Shinhen Shinmyou Sutra, the Local Shinto Shinmyou Sutra, and the Jingen Shinryoku Shinmyou Sutra.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=236}} These sutras were said to be the teachings of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Tenji-Yane|en}}, but these three sutras are fictitious and there is no evidence that they were ever produced.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=239}} Kanetu forged sutras similar to these by posing as the authors, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en}}, to create his own sutras.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=239-240}} The history of the sanctuary was also created by Kaneku himself.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=240}} Yoshida Shinto also established the ritual of Shinto funeral rites, in which people are worshipped as gods. Since ancient times, Shinto has not been very involved in funeral rituals due to the custom of viewing death as {{ill|Kegare|Stain|en}}, and examples of enshrining deceased people as gods were limited to forms such as grudge worship and Tenjin worship to appease grudges. However, in Yoshida Shinto, where people and gods are considered to be closely related, funeral rituals were actively practiced, and Yoshida Kento built a Shinryu-sha, a spiritual shrine, over the remains of the deceased.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=186-187}} Although Yoshida Shinto was an emerging force, it rapidly rose to prominence, perhaps due to the social unrest of the age of war, and was widely accepted, especially by the upper classes, as it received the support of {{ill|Hino Tomiko|en}} in the construction of the Omoto Shrine, and even received the imperial approval of the Omoto Shrine in {{ill|1473|en}} ({{ill|Bunmei|en}}5).{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=235}}、The center of the Shinto world in modern times.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=244}} On the other hand, we have received strong protests from the shrines of both domestic and foreign shrines at Ise Shrine.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=243}} Yoshida Shinto is the first Shinto theory to have its own doctrines, scriptures, and rituals independent of Buddhism, while integrating various religious discourses in a cross-border manner.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=243}}、The Shinto scholar {{ill|Okada Chuangji|ja|岡田莊司}} described the establishment of Yoshida Shinto as "a turning point in the history of Shinto.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=17}}、The historian {{ill|Toshio Kuroda|en}} argues that the establishment of Yoshida Shinto was the establishment of Shinto{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=16}}It is considered by several researchers to be a turning point in the history of Shinto. As mentioned above, Yoshida Shinto, which established Shinto funeral rites, became involved in the construction of shrines that enshrined warring feudal lords as gods in the Warring States period, and Kanemi Yoshida was involved in the construction of {{ill|Toyokuni Shrine (Kyoto)|lt=Toyokuni Shrine|en}}, which enshrined {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en}} as a god. Shinryuin Bonshun of the Yoshida family taught Shinto to {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en}}, and according to his will, conducted a Shinto funeral service after Ieyasu's death.{{Cite web |last=鎌田純一 |date=2017-10-19 |title=梵舜 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%A2%B5%E8%88%9C-135079 |access-date=2021-07-06 |publisher=コトバンク（日本大百科全書）}}(However, {{ill|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|en}} became the {{ill|Sanno Shinto|en}} style after {{ill|Tenkai|en}} won the debate). === Early modern times === ==== Restoration of the Shogunate's Shinto System and Imperial Rites ==== When the era of warfare ended and the Edo period began, the administration of shrines was reorganized. The shogunate first relieved each shrine of its current territory and granted it the privilege of "not entering into the custody of the guardian. However, what was granted was the right to make profits from the shrines, and the ownership of the land belonged to the shogunate.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=191}} The {{ill|Shogun|lt=Shogunate|en}} also established the {{ill|Jisha-bugyō|en}} as a position reporting directly to the shogun, and placed it at the head of the three magistrates, surpassing the {{ill|Machi-bugyō|lt=Town Magistrate|en}} and {{ill|Kanjō-bugyō|lt=Account Magistrate|en}} under the jurisdiction of the {{ill|Rōjū|lt=Rōchū|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=191-192}} In addition, a Shinto department under the jurisdiction of the temple and shrine magistrates was established to study the truths of Shinto and the rituals of rituals and to respond to the advice of the temple and shrine magistrates.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=192}}On the other hand, individual magistrates were assigned to specific shrines, such as {{ill|Yamada bugyō|en}}, who was in charge of Ise Shrine, and Nikko bugyō, who was in charge of {{ill|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|lt=Nikko Tōshō-gū|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=198}} In {{ill|1665|en}} (the fifth year of the {{ill|Kanbun (era)|lt=Kanbun|en}}), the shogunate issued the Priest Law for Priests of Various Shrines, which stated that ordinary {{ill|Kannushi|lt=Priests|en}} without rank must obtain a Shinto license issued by the Yoshida family before they can wear a hunting robe or crown, giving the Yoshida family control over almost all priests.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=192-196}} However, it was approved that those families that had been conferred ranks by the Imperial Court through transmission, such as the Jingu Shrine, {{ill|Kamo Shrine|en}}, {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}, {{ill|Usa Jingū|en}}, {{ill|Izumo-taisha|en}}, and {{ill|Fushimi Inari-taisha|en}}, would continue to use the same methods as before, without the Yoshida family.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=193}} In addition, the law stipulates penalties for neglect of duties by priests, prohibition of sales and purchases of shrine property, and the obligation to repair shrine buildings. As for funerals, the shogunate enforced that funerals be held at dannaji temples in conjunction with the creation of the sect's personnel register, and people were obliged to hold Buddhist funerals.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=127}} In this case, the shrine, not the temple, proved that the Christians were not Christians, so it was called "Shinto Shinto Shinto" instead of "Temple Shinto.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=127}} The Shogunate also financially supported the partial revival of the imperial rituals that had been suspended due to warfare. After 222 years of interruptions since {{ill|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|en}}, the Dai-namesai was revived in the reign of {{ill|Emperor Higashiyama|en}}, and became a regular event since {{ill|Emperor Sakuramachi|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} The {{ill|Niiname-no-Matsuri|en}} was also revived in {{ill|1688|en}} (the first year of {{ill|Genroku|en}}), the year after the restoration of the Dai-namesai.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} In {{ill|1744|en}} (the first year of {{ill|Enkyō (Edo period)|Enkyo|en}}), some of the votive offerings were also revived, including those to {{ill|Twenty-Two Shrines|en}} and to Usa Hachiman Shrine and {{ill|Kashii-gū|lt=Kashii Shrine|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} The Imperial Court's dispatch of imperial envoys on the occasion of the Shinnamesai festival was revived in {{ill|1647|en}} (the fourth year of the {{ill|Shōhō|lt=Shohoho|en}}) by the special order of {{ill|Emperor Go-Kōmyō|en}}. The ceremonial relocation of the Ise Jingu Shrine was also suspended, but was rebuilt during the {{ill|Azuchi-Momoyama period|lt2=Orifuji administration|en}} thanks to the efforts of Seisun and Shuyou of Keikoin. The {{ill|Department of Divinities|en}}, which was destroyed by fire during the war, was replaced by the eight temples at the Yoshida Shrine, and the Divinities themselves were not rebuilt.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=190-191}} The Shogunate also imposed restrictions on Shugendo, and in {{ill|1613|en}} ({{ill|Keichō|en}}18) issued the "Shugendo Hōdō," which stated that yamabushi must belong to either the Tōzan or Honzan sects, and forbade those who did not.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=126}} The latter played a leading role in folk beliefs such as {{ill|Koshin-do|en}}.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=126}} ==== The establishment of Confucian Shinto ==== {{Main|Confucian Shinto}} During the Edo period, while Buddhism took its place as the state religion under the {{ill|Danka system|wlt=Terashi system|en}}, ideologically it stagnated as a whole.{{Sfn|Mori Kazuya|2018|p=169}}In the world of thought, it was effective as an ideology to support the Shogunate system. In the world of thought, Confucianism, especially {{ill|Cheng-Zhu school|en}}, which was effective as an ideology to support the shogunate system and preached human ethics compatible with the secularism of the Edo period, flourished very much, while Buddhism was criticized by Confucians for its worldliness that was incompatible with secular ethics. Buddhism was criticized by Confucians for its worldly ethics.{{Sfn|Mori Kazuya|2018|p=76}} The mainstream theories of Shinto also shifted from Shinto and Buddhism to {{ill|Confucian Shinto|en}}, which was more closely linked to Confucianism. Although there were theories of Shinto advocated by the {{ill|Yangmingism|en}} school, such as {{ill|Nakae Tōju|en}}'s Taikyō Shinto, most of the theories of Shinto were formed by Shūji. Although Confucian thought was also incorporated in the idea of Shinto, Confucian Shinto differs in that it explicitly criticized Buddhism and attempted to escape its influence. On the other hand, the logical structure of the Confucian Shinto inherited a strong medieval esoteric tradition, and the Buddhist theory of Shinto-Buddhist syncretism was replaced by the Shuko theory, which can be said to be in a transitional period between the medieval and early modern periods.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=501-504}} [[File:Razan_Hayashi.jpg|thumb|Lin Luoshan, a pioneer of Confucian Shinto]] The pioneer of Confucian Shinto was {{ill|Hayashi Razan|en}}. In addition to spreading his knowledge of Zhu Xi to Japan, Razan also studied Shinto, and wrote such works as "Shinto Denju" and "Honcho Jinja Ko", forming his own theory of Shinto called Rituji Shinto. The idea was that the Confucian god {{ill|Li (neo-Confucianism)|lt=Li|en}} was the same as the Shinto god, and that the ultimate god was {{ill|Kuni-no-Tokotachi|lt=Kuni-Tokotachi|en}}.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=510-519}} While advocating Shinto and anti-Buddhism, claiming that Japan was pure and superior before the introduction of Buddhism, he also claimed that {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en}} was a descendant of Taihaku based on {{ill|Sinocentrism|lt=Chinese thought|en}}, and that the {{ill|Imperial Regalia of Japan|en}}, claiming that the {{ill|Three Sacred Treasures|en}} represented the three virtues of Confucianism, and tried to appeal to the high level of Japanese civilization by claiming that Japan has belonged to the Chinese sphere since ancient times.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=510-519}} In addition, the essence of Shinto is a political doctrine that has been handed down from Amaterasu to successive emperors, and rituals at ordinary shrines and festivals for common people were dismissed as "toshu-zuyaku Shinto" and mere "actors.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=510-519}} In the case of Yoshida Shinto, Yoshikawa Tadashi, a merchant, was initiated into the Yoshida family, and was granted the "Shinto Dotosho" by Hagiwara Kanetsugu, the head of the Yoshida family, and became the official successor. He formed Yoshikawa Shinto, which removed Buddhist discourse from Yoshida Shinto and incorporated more Confucian teachings. His philosophy was that Shinto is the source of all laws and that Kunitokotachi-no-Mikoto presides over the world, and that the world and human beings are created by "truth," which is the same as God. However, because the clarity and wisdom of the Divine Light is clouded by the contamination of the human mind, it is necessary to return to the original form through tsutsumi.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=522-528}} And as a concrete way to do this, he taught that we should perform purification to purify the inside and outside, express our sincerity by performing ritual rites, and pray to the gods.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=522-528}} In addition, the Confucian view of the Five Luns is that God has given man a mission, and that the relationship between sovereign and vassal is the most important.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=522-528}} In Ise Shinto, the late Ise Shinto, which excluded Buddhism and incorporated Confucianism, was formed in the Edo period by Nobuka Deguchi, a Shinto priest. The essence of Shinto, he wrote, is the way that Japanese people should naturally conduct themselves in their daily lives, the "way of daily use," which is to perform one's duties with honesty and purity of mind. He pointed out that it is a mistake to think that only the rituals at shrines, such as chanting congratulatory prayers and holding ball-shaped sticks, are Shinto.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=533-541}} In addition, he criticized the use of Confucianism and Buddhism for the purpose of learning, arguing that although all religions are ultimately the same, and there are many points of agreement between Shinto and Confucianism, the systems and customs of each country differ, and therefore Japanese people should respect the laws and customs of Japan.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=533-541}} However, he also stated that it is okay to study Confucianism and Buddhism as long as Shinto is placed at the center. He argued that prohibiting Buddhism and Confucianism because of their harmful effects and destroying current customs is against the natural order of things and is different from Shinto.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=533-541}} [[File:Yamazaki_Ansai.jpg|left|thumb|Yaksai Yamazaki, the culmination of Confucian Shinto]] These Confucian theories of Shinto were compiled by {{ill|Yamazaki Ansai|en}}. After making a name for himself as a Confucian scholar, he was taken in by {{ill|Hoshina Masayuki|en}}, Lord of the {{ill|Aizu Domain|en}}, where he came into contact with Masayuki's guest teacher, Yoshikawa Tadashi, and learned Yoshikawa Shinto, leading to the creation of his own Taruka Shinto. The idea was to combine {{ill|Kamiyonanayo|lt=Seven Generations of the Divine Age|en}} with the {{ill|Neo-Confucianism|en}} of the Shuzi school, and to believe that Kunitokotachi-no-Mikoto was the {{ill|Taiji (philosophy)|lt=Taiji|en}}, and that the five gods that arose after him were {{ill|Wuxing (Chinese philosophy)|lt=Five Elements|en}}, and that the last two, {{ill|Izanagi|en}} and {{ill|Izanami|en}}, combined the Five Elements to give birth to the land, gods, and people. The spirit of the god who created the people resides in each person, and the gods and people are in a state of union called "the only way of heaven and man.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=545-550}} He said that Shinto means that people should live according to God, and that people should pray to God to obtain blessings, but that people must be "honest" in order to do so, and that "respect" is the first thing to realize this "honesty.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=545-550}} The relationship between the sovereign and the vassal is not one of rivalry or power, but one of unity, and the sovereign and the vassal have protected the country through their mutual protection.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=545-550}}、He also had a great influence on the later philosophy of the Emperor. After the death of Yaksai Yamazaki, his pupil Shoshinmachi Kimimichi succeeded him, and the Taruka Shinto sect reached its zenith, spreading throughout the country, especially in Edo and Kyoto, widely spreading among nobles, warriors, and priests, and having the greatest influence on the Shinto world.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=551-554}} After the death of Masamichi, his disciple, Masahide Tamaki, succeeded him and organized the single, double, triple, and quadruple mysteries based on the "Mochijusho" written by Masamichi, and worked on the organization of the Taruka Shinto.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=551-554}} Some people, such as Gousai Wakabayashi, criticized this move to make the teachings secret, saying that it would obscure Yaksai's true intentions.{{Sfn|Kokugakuin University Institute of Japanese Culture|1999|pp=437-439|loc=垂加神道（西岡和彦）}} In addition to the Tachibana family Shinto mentioned above, the Hakka Shinto and Tsuchimikado Shinto were organized under the influence of the Taruka Shinto. Yoshimi Yukikazu, who was one of Tamaki Masahide's pupils, wrote a book entitled "Goubu-shosetsu-ben" in which he criticized Ise Shinto and Yoshida Shinto by arguing that the Shinto Goubu-shosetsu was a fake book from the Middle Ages, and also criticized Taruka Shinto, which also used the Goubu-shosetsu as its scriptures.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=551-554}} In fact, after Masahide Tamaki, Taraka Shinto began to stagnate ideologically and surrendered its mainstream position to {{ill|Kokugaku|en}}.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=551-554}} In conjunction with these anti-Buddhist ideological trends, a movement to separate Shinto and Buddhism began to spread in some of the clans that had accepted Confucian Shinto. In the {{ill|Mito Domain|en}}, {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en}} investigated the history of shrines with strong Shinto-Buddhist practices in {{ill|1696|en}} (the 9th year of the {{ill|Genroku|en}}), and organized them in such a way as to wipe out the Buddhist flavor. In addition, Masayuki Hoshina of the Aizu domain carried out a similar reorganization of temples and shrines.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=128}} In addition, {{ill|Ikeda Mitsumasa|en}} of the {{ill|Okayama Domain|en}} promoted the return of priests from the {{ill|Nichiren-shū|en}} {{ill|Fuju-fuse|en}} and Tendai and Shingon sects, reducing the number of temples and encouraging Shinto funerals.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=128}} In {{ill|1647|en}}, {{ill|Matsue Domain|en}}, under the leadership of {{ill|Matsue Domain|en}} lord Matsudaira Naomasa, Buddhist elements were removed from the {{ill|Izumo-taisha|en}}.{{Cite journal|last=Teeuwen|first=Mark|last2=Zhong|first2=Yijiang|date=2017|title=Izumo, Ise, and Modern Shinto|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/90017702|journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies|volume=44|issue=2|pages=325–332|issn=0304-1042}} === Meiji Restoration === In 1869 during the [[Meiji {{Draft}}{{Promising draft}} {{Expand Japanese}} [[en:draft:Yoshida family]] [[ja:吉田家]] {{Infobox Japanese clan|province of origin=[[Yamashiro Province]]|home province=[[Yamashiro Province]]|founder={{ill|Ame no Koyane|en}} (Urabe)
{{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}} (Yoshida)|image=File:Yoshida torii sakura 03.jpg|caption=Izumo Taisha, the traditional shrine of the family|parent house=[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]|image caption=[[Yoshida Shrine]], the traditional shrine of the family|alt=[[Yoshida Shrine]], the traditional shrine of the family}} The {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Yoshida clan|ja|吉田家|en|draft:Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family}} ([[:ja:吉田家|吉田家]]) also known as the {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|en|draft:Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family}} ([[:ja:卜部氏|卜部氏]]) were a family of diviners in Japan{{Cite web |title=Yoshida family {{!}} Encyclopedia.com |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/yoshida-family |access-date=2023-03-12 |website=www.encyclopedia.com}}. They were highly influential in the development of Shinto. The historical {{ill|Yoshida Shinto|en}} school of thought which was the norm until the [[Meiji Restoration]] is named after them.{{Cite web|date=2024-03-19|title=Yoshida Shintō {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151532/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9901|access-date=2024-03-19|website=web.archive.org}} They were originally the diviners of the Department of divinities under the Urabe clan name. They served at [[Yoshida Shrine|Yoshida Shrine]], their traditional shrine and namesake.{{Cite web|title=Yoshida family|url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686?d=%2F10.1093%2Foi%2Fauthority.20110803125403686&p=emailAMFctfco71wyE|access-date=2024-03-19|website=Oxford Reference|language=en|doi=10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686?d=/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686&p=emailamfctfco71wye}} == Urabe clan == The Urabe (卜部) clan is a clan whose name is "Urabe." They were one of the ancient ritual aristocrats, specializing in fortune-telling to determine good or bad outcomes. == Contents == 1. Overview 2. Urabe of Izu (伊豆卜部) 3. Urabe of Iki (壱岐卜部) 4. Urabe of Tsushima (対馬卜部) 5. Urabe Serving Shrines    1. Urabe of Kashima Shrine (Hitachi Province)    2. Urabe of Katsuragi Hitotoshi Shrine (Yamato Province)    3. Urabe of Munakata Shrine (Chikuzen Province) 6. Other Urabe 7. Footnote    1. Annotation    2. Reference 8. References == Summary == Urabe is a clan whose occupation was Kameboku (divination by interpreting the cracks formed when a tortoise shell is burned). Different lineages of Urabe clans exist across Japan, with those from Izu (伊豆), Iki (壱岐), and Tsushima (対馬) appointed as officials of the Jingikan (神祇官). The Izu Urabe clan was appointed as vice-ministers (大副 and 少副) of the Jingikan, with 5 people from Izu, 5 from Iki, and 10 from Tsushima appointed to lower-ranking official positions, recognized for their excellence in divination techniques. It is said that Urabe clans not from these three regions are descendants of clans related to Taizan (太占), an ancient form of Japanese divination. == Urabe of Izu == - Surname: From Sukune Urabe (宿禰卜部) to Asaomi Urabe (朝臣卜部) - Ancestor: Hiramaro Urabe (平麻呂卜部) - Descendants include Kaneyoshi Urabe (兼好卜部) - The actual ancestor, Hiramaro Urabe, served in the early Heian period, but details before him are unclear. There are genealogies suggesting Hiramaro was the son of Onakatomi Chijimaro (大中臣千治麿), a grandson of Onakatomi Kiyomaro (大中臣清麿), but these are considered later fabrications. It is theorized they served Mishima Taisha Shrine (三嶋大社) as priests. The surname was changed from Sukune to Asaomi by Yoshida Kanehiro (吉田兼煕) in 1375. The descendants of Hiramaro split into the Yoshida-sha (吉田社) and Hirano-sha (平野社) lineages, serving alternately as Jingi Dai-Vice and Jingi Sho-Vice. == Urabe of Iki == The Iki Urabe clan, associated with Iyoshi Island (伊吉島). Genealogies indicate Maneko no Mikoto (真根子命), a descendant of Raijin no Mikoto (雷神命) and part of Empress Jingu's (神功皇后) retinue, as an ancestor. Despite some claims to Nakatomi (中臣) lineage, discrepancies in genealogical records suggest different origins. == Urabe of Tsushima == The Tsushima Urabe clan, associated with the Tsushima Prefecture (対馬府) ruling family. Ancestral origins vary across historical sources, including deities like Takehiradori no Mikoto (建比良鳥命) and Raidaijin no Mikoto (雷大臣命). == Urabe Serving Shrines == - **Kashima Shrine (鹿嶋神宮) in Hitachi Province:** Served from ancient times, involved in divination. - **Katsuragi Hitotoshi Shrine (葛城一言主神社) in Yamato Province:** Ancestor served as a priest. - **Munakata Shrine (宗像大社) in Chikuzen Province:** Ancestors served, later becoming vassals of the Kuroda clan (黒田氏). == Other Urabe == Beyond the mentioned, the Urabe surname appears in ancient and Nara period records across regions like Mutsu (陸奥), Shimousa (下総), Suruga (駿河), Omi (近江), and Inaba (因幡) Provinces. == History == {{Main|en:History of Shinto}} The origins of the Yoshida family date back to the [[Heian period]] or earlier. They claimed descent from {{ill|Ame no Koyane|en}}.{{rp|25-26}} It is believed that originally the Urabe clan was a low clan subordinate to the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏|en||simple|User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan}}.{{Cite web|date=2024-03-19|title=Jingi shizoku {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151546/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9925|access-date=2024-04-01|website=web.archive.org}} They initially played support roles in rituals such as {{ill|Ōharae-shiki|en}}, but over time they expanded and managed to gain more power by monopolizing the role of ''miyaji'' until eventually becoming nearly in charge of the [[Department of Divinities]] as a whole. === Early history === In the {{ill|Department of Divinities|department of divinities|en}} there was this organization.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_Q81DQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto: A History|last=Hardacre|first=Helen|date=2017|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-062171-1|language=en}}{{rp|35}}.{{rp|25-26}} * The {{ill|Inbe clan|Inbe family|en||simple}} was responsible for managing the procuring materials for rituals and performing abstinence rites.{{rp|25-26}} and distribution of tribute offerings within the Jingikan..{{rp|35}} claiming descent from Ame no [[Futodama]] no Mikoto..{{rp|25-26}} * {{ill|Sarume clan|lt=Sarume family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|en:draft|6=ja|7=猿女君|8=fr|9=Clan Sarume}} women were tasked with performing sacred dances..{{rp|35}} Initially serving as seers and healers, their role evolved to include performing ritual dances, or kagura, during Enthronement Rites and court ceremonies..{{rp|25-26}} claiming descent from the goddess [[Ama-no-Uzume|Ame no Uzume]] no Mikoto..{{rp|25-26}} * The Tamatsukuri specialized in the creation of jewels..{{rp|35}} * The Kagamitsukuri were known for crafting {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=bronze mirrors|en}} for use in shrine ceremonies..{{rp|35}} * The {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|en|draft:Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family}} ([[:ja:卜部氏|卜部氏]]) considered to be of relatively low rank, carried out divination practices..{{rp|35}}{{Cite web|title=Jingidoke|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151308/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9910|access-date=2024-03-19|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} using tortoise shells and deer scapulae {{rp|25-26}} later taking the surname {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Yoshida|ja|吉田家|en|draft:Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family}} and claiming descent from Ame no Koyane..{{rp|25-26}} * {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏|en||simple|User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan}}: Later known as the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|lt=Fujiwara|en}}, they specialized in reciting prayers to the Kami, with a divine lineage tracing back to {{ill|Ame no Koyane|en}} no Mikoto..{{rp|25-26}} ** In his book ''Jinja to kodai ōken saishi'' (1989). {{Interlanguage link multi|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup}} goes on to theorize that the {{Nihongo|{{ill|Ō clan|lt=Ō clan|ja|多氏}}|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}} was originally {{Nihongo|ōmi|大忌|"greater taboo (priesthood)"}}, but was usurped by the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏|en||simple|User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan}} who were among the "lesser priesthood" (the latter claims descent from the {{Nihongo|[[Inbe clan]]|[[:ja:忌部氏|忌部氏]]}}). ** Takemikazuchi was originally a local god (''kuni-tsu-kami'') revered by the {{Nihongo|{{ill|Ō clan|lt=Ō clan|ja|多氏}}|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}},{{cite book |last=小向 |first=正司 |title=神道の本 |publisher=学研 |year=1992 |series=Books Esoterica |volume=2 |pages=76–7}}(zasshi code 66951-07; kyōtsu zasshi code T10-66951-07-1000) and was a god of maritime travel. However, the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏|en||simple|User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan}} who also has roots in this region, and when they took over control of priestly duties from the Ō clan, they also instituted Takemikazuchi as the Nakatomi clan's [[ujigami]] (clan deity). Or so this is the observation by {{Interlanguage link multi|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup}} {{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}} was the first person to have the name Yoshida, taken from [[Yoshida Shrine]] which he ran. The Yoshida faimly grew immensely powerful later. === Formation of Yoshida Shinto === {{Main|Yoshida Shintō}} [[File:吉田兼倶肖像画.jpg|thumb|Yoshida Kanetomo]] During the {{ill|Ōnin|en}} reign, the {{ill|Ōnin War|en}} broke out and Kyoto was burnt to the ground, affecting many temples and shrines, and causing the abortion of imperial court rituals such as the Ōnin Festival and the coronation ceremony. One of the priests who was shocked by the upheaval was {{ill|Yoshida Kanetomo|en}}. Kanetomo, who was so upset that he lost his own {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}} to the war, as well as more than a dozen residents of the area around the shrine.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=182}} However, the loss of many ancient manuscripts due to the war led to the formation of a new Shinto theory called {{ill|Yoshida Shintō|en}}.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=234}} The {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Yoshida family|ja|吉田家}}, whose surname is {{ill|Radical 25|lt=Turabu|en|}}, was a family that specialized in Ketu (divination) in the Ministry of Divine Worship and succeeded to the position of Deputy Minister of Divine Worship for many generations. In the Middle Ages, {{ill|Urabe Kanekata|ja|卜部兼方}} became well versed in the study of the Chronicles of Japan, writing {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|en}}, and was called the "House of the Chronicles of Japan.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=181}}{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9861|access-date=2024-03-25|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} Kanetsu wrote "Shinto Taioi" and "Onna Shinto Meibyo Shu" to compile medieval Shinto thought, while incorporating discourses from various religions to present a new Shinto theory called "Yoshida Shinto". In the book, he classified Shinto into three categories: "Honjaku Enki Shinto" (auspicious signs handed down from shrine to shrine), "Ryobu Nariai Shinto", and "Motomune Sougen Shinto". He stated that the "Motomune Sougen Shinto" handed down by his family was the legitimate Shinto since the dawn of Japan, and defined God as "the spiritual head of heaven, earth and all things" and the Way as "the origin of all things and all actions".{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=236-237}} With regard to the relationship between Shinto, {{ill|Confucianism|en}} and {{ill|Buddhism|en}}, he strongly advocated the theory that Shinto was the root, [[Confucianism]] emerged as a branch and leaf in [[China]], and [[Buddhism]] blossomed as a fruit in [[India]].{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=113}} [[File:Yoshida_shrine_funeral_hall.jpg|left|thumb|{{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}} in {{ill|Sakyō-ku, Kyoto|lt=Sakyo-ku|en}} {{ill|Kyoto|Kyoto City|en}}]] He argued that Shinto has three aspects: "body," which is the essence, "aspect," which is the manifestation, and "use," which is the action, and that these actions govern all phenomena such as the sun and moon, cold and heat, and nature. In the end, Kaneku's theory of Shinto was a kind of pantheism in which God exists within all beings, and God is omnipresent throughout the universe.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=237-238}} Kaneku formed many rituals along with his Shinto theories. First, he established the Omotoshae Shrine in the precincts of {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}}, which he proclaimed to be the place of worship for the Inner Shrine, Outer Shrine, eight temples, and more than 3,000 Shinto shrines, the root of Shinto rituals in Japan since the time of Jimmu, and the main shrine of all Shinto shrines in Japan.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=235-236}} In addition, under the influence of esoteric Buddhism, he invented the {{ill|Homa (ritual)|lt=Homa|en}} event, in which a fire is kindled in an octagonal platform with a furnace at its center, and grain and porridge are thrown into the fire while praying, forming the San-dan event along with the 18 Shinto events and Sougen Shinto events.{{Cite web |title=吉田神道行事壇 |url=http://museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/exhibition/detail/id=4 |access-date=2021-03-02 |publisher=國學院大學博物館}} These teachings were expounded by the "Three Nerves" of the Tengen Shinhen Shinmyou Sutra, the Local Shinto Shinmyou Sutra, and the Jingen Shinryoku Shinmyou Sutra.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=236}} These sutras were said to be the teachings of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Tenji-Yane|en}}, but these three sutras are fictitious and there is no evidence that they were ever produced.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=239}} Kanetu forged sutras similar to these by posing as the authors, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en}}, to create his own sutras.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=239-240}} The history of the sanctuary was also created by Kaneku himself.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=240}} Yoshida Shinto also established the ritual of Shinto funeral rites, in which people are worshipped as gods. Since ancient times, Shinto has not been very involved in funeral rituals due to the custom of viewing death as {{ill|Kegare|Stain|en}}, and examples of enshrining deceased people as gods were limited to forms such as grudge worship and Tenjin worship to appease grudges. However, in Yoshida Shinto, where people and gods are considered to be closely related, funeral rituals were actively practiced, and Yoshida Kento built a Shinryu-sha, a spiritual shrine, over the remains of the deceased.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=186-187}} Although Yoshida Shinto was an emerging force, it rapidly rose to prominence, perhaps due to the social unrest of the age of war, and was widely accepted, especially by the upper classes, as it received the support of {{ill|Hino Tomiko|en}} in the construction of the Omoto Shrine, and even received the imperial approval of the Omoto Shrine in {{ill|1473|en}} ({{ill|Bunmei|en}}5).{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=235}}、The center of the Shinto world in modern times.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=244}} On the other hand, we have received strong protests from the shrines of both domestic and foreign shrines at Ise Shrine.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=243}} Yoshida Shinto is the first Shinto theory to have its own doctrines, scriptures, and rituals independent of Buddhism, while integrating various religious discourses in a cross-border manner.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=243}}、The Shinto scholar {{ill|Okada Chuangji|ja|岡田莊司}} described the establishment of Yoshida Shinto as "a turning point in the history of Shinto.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=17}}、The historian {{ill|Toshio Kuroda|en}} argues that the establishment of Yoshida Shinto was the establishment of Shinto{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=16}}It is considered by several researchers to be a turning point in the history of Shinto. As mentioned above, Yoshida Shinto, which established Shinto funeral rites, became involved in the construction of shrines that enshrined warring feudal lords as gods in the Warring States period, and Kanemi Yoshida was involved in the construction of {{ill|Toyokuni Shrine (Kyoto)|lt=Toyokuni Shrine|en}}, which enshrined {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en}} as a god. Shinryuin Bonshun of the Yoshida family taught Shinto to {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en}}, and according to his will, conducted a Shinto funeral service after Ieyasu's death.{{Cite web |last=鎌田純一 |date=2017-10-19 |title=梵舜 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%A2%B5%E8%88%9C-135079 |access-date=2021-07-06 |publisher=コトバンク（日本大百科全書）}}(However, {{ill|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|en}} became the {{ill|Sanno Shinto|en}} style after {{ill|Tenkai|en}} won the debate). === Early modern times === ==== Restoration of the Shogunate's Shinto System and Imperial Rites ==== When the era of warfare ended and the Edo period began, the administration of shrines was reorganized. The shogunate first relieved each shrine of its current territory and granted it the privilege of "not entering into the custody of the guardian. However, what was granted was the right to make profits from the shrines, and the ownership of the land belonged to the shogunate.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=191}} The {{ill|Shogun|lt=Shogunate|en}} also established the {{ill|Jisha-bugyō|en}} as a position reporting directly to the shogun, and placed it at the head of the three magistrates, surpassing the {{ill|Machi-bugyō|lt=Town Magistrate|en}} and {{ill|Kanjō-bugyō|lt=Account Magistrate|en}} under the jurisdiction of the {{ill|Rōjū|lt=Rōchū|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=191-192}} In addition, a Shinto department under the jurisdiction of the temple and shrine magistrates was established to study the truths of Shinto and the rituals of rituals and to respond to the advice of the temple and shrine magistrates.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=192}}On the other hand, individual magistrates were assigned to specific shrines, such as {{ill|Yamada bugyō|en}}, who was in charge of Ise Shrine, and Nikko bugyō, who was in charge of {{ill|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|lt=Nikko Tōshō-gū|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=198}} In {{ill|1665|en}} (the fifth year of the {{ill|Kanbun (era)|lt=Kanbun|en}}), the shogunate issued the Priest Law for Priests of Various Shrines, which stated that ordinary {{ill|Kannushi|lt=Priests|en}} without rank must obtain a Shinto license issued by the Yoshida family before they can wear a hunting robe or crown, giving the Yoshida family control over almost all priests.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=192-196}} However, it was approved that those families that had been conferred ranks by the Imperial Court through transmission, such as the Jingu Shrine, {{ill|Kamo Shrine|en}}, {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}, {{ill|Usa Jingū|en}}, {{ill|Izumo-taisha|en}}, and {{ill|Fushimi Inari-taisha|en}}, would continue to use the same methods as before, without the Yoshida family.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=193}} In addition, the law stipulates penalties for neglect of duties by priests, prohibition of sales and purchases of shrine property, and the obligation to repair shrine buildings. As for funerals, the shogunate enforced that funerals be held at dannaji temples in conjunction with the creation of the sect's personnel register, and people were obliged to hold Buddhist funerals.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=127}} In this case, the shrine, not the temple, proved that the Christians were not Christians, so it was called "Shinto Shinto Shinto" instead of "Temple Shinto.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=127}} The Shogunate also financially supported the partial revival of the imperial rituals that had been suspended due to warfare. After 222 years of interruptions since {{ill|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|en}}, the Dai-namesai was revived in the reign of {{ill|Emperor Higashiyama|en}}, and became a regular event since {{ill|Emperor Sakuramachi|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} The {{ill|Niiname-no-Matsuri|en}} was also revived in {{ill|1688|en}} (the first year of {{ill|Genroku|en}}), the year after the restoration of the Dai-namesai.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} In {{ill|1744|en}} (the first year of {{ill|Enkyō (Edo period)|Enkyo|en}}), some of the votive offerings were also revived, including those to {{ill|Twenty-Two Shrines|en}} and to Usa Hachiman Shrine and {{ill|Kashii-gū|lt=Kashii Shrine|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} The Imperial Court's dispatch of imperial envoys on the occasion of the Shinnamesai festival was revived in {{ill|1647|en}} (the fourth year of the {{ill|Shōhō|lt=Shohoho|en}}) by the special order of {{ill|Emperor Go-Kōmyō|en}}. The ceremonial relocation of the Ise Jingu Shrine was also suspended, but was rebuilt during the {{ill|Azuchi-Momoyama period|lt2=Orifuji administration|en}} thanks to the efforts of Seisun and Shuyou of Keikoin. The {{ill|Department of Divinities|en}}, which was destroyed by fire during the war, was replaced by the eight temples at the Yoshida Shrine, and the Divinities themselves were not rebuilt.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=190-191}} The Shogunate also imposed restrictions on Shugendo, and in {{ill|1613|en}} ({{ill|Keichō|en}}18) issued the "Shugendo Hōdō," which stated that yamabushi must belong to either the Tōzan or Honzan sects, and forbade those who did not.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=126}} The latter played a leading role in folk beliefs such as {{ill|Koshin-do|en}}.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=126}} ==== The establishment of Confucian Shinto ==== {{Main|Confucian Shinto}} During the Edo period, while Buddhism took its place as the state religion under the {{ill|Danka system|wlt=Terashi system|en}}, ideologically it stagnated as a whole.{{Sfn|Mori Kazuya|2018|p=169}}In the world of thought, it was effective as an ideology to support the Shogunate system. In the world of thought, Confucianism, especially {{ill|Cheng-Zhu school|en}}, which was effective as an ideology to support the shogunate system and preached human ethics compatible with the secularism of the Edo period, flourished very much, while Buddhism was criticized by Confucians for its worldliness that was incompatible with secular ethics. Buddhism was criticized by Confucians for its worldly ethics.{{Sfn|Mori Kazuya|2018|p=76}} The mainstream theories of Shinto also shifted from Shinto and Buddhism to {{ill|Confucian Shinto|en}}, which was more closely linked to Confucianism. Although there were theories of Shinto advocated by the {{ill|Yangmingism|en}} school, such as {{ill|Nakae Tōju|en}}'s Taikyō Shinto, most of the theories of Shinto were formed by Shūji. Although Confucian thought was also incorporated in the idea of Shinto, Confucian Shinto differs in that it explicitly criticized Buddhism and attempted to escape its influence. On the other hand, the logical structure of the Confucian Shinto inherited a strong medieval esoteric tradition, and the Buddhist theory of Shinto-Buddhist syncretism was replaced by the Shuko theory, which can be said to be in a transitional period between the medieval and early modern periods.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=501-504}} [[File:Razan_Hayashi.jpg|thumb|Lin Luoshan, a pioneer of Confucian Shinto]] The pioneer of Confucian Shinto was {{ill|Hayashi Razan|en}}. In addition to spreading his knowledge of Zhu Xi to Japan, Razan also studied Shinto, and wrote such works as "Shinto Denju" and "Honcho Jinja Ko", forming his own theory of Shinto called Rituji Shinto. The idea was that the Confucian god {{ill|Li (neo-Confucianism)|lt=Li|en}} was the same as the Shinto god, and that the ultimate god was {{ill|Kuni-no-Tokotachi|lt=Kuni-Tokotachi|en}}.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=510-519}} While advocating Shinto and anti-Buddhism, claiming that Japan was pure and superior before the introduction of Buddhism, he also claimed that {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en}} was a descendant of Taihaku based on {{ill|Sinocentrism|lt=Chinese thought|en}}, and that the {{ill|Imperial Regalia of Japan|en}}, claiming that the {{ill|Three Sacred Treasures|en}} represented the three virtues of Confucianism, and tried to appeal to the high level of Japanese civilization by claiming that Japan has belonged to the Chinese sphere since ancient times.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=510-519}} In addition, the essence of Shinto is a political doctrine that has been handed down from Amaterasu to successive emperors, and rituals at ordinary shrines and festivals for common people were dismissed as "toshu-zuyaku Shinto" and mere "actors.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=510-519}} In the case of Yoshida Shinto, Yoshikawa Tadashi, a merchant, was initiated into the Yoshida family, and was granted the "Shinto Dotosho" by Hagiwara Kanetsugu, the head of the Yoshida family, and became the official successor. He formed Yoshikawa Shinto, which removed Buddhist discourse from Yoshida Shinto and incorporated more Confucian teachings. His philosophy was that Shinto is the source of all laws and that Kunitokotachi-no-Mikoto presides over the world, and that the world and human beings are created by "truth," which is the same as God. However, because the clarity and wisdom of the Divine Light is clouded by the contamination of the human mind, it is necessary to return to the original form through tsutsumi.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=522-528}} And as a concrete way to do this, he taught that we should perform purification to purify the inside and outside, express our sincerity by performing ritual rites, and pray to the gods.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=522-528}} In addition, the Confucian view of the Five Luns is that God has given man a mission, and that the relationship between sovereign and vassal is the most important.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=522-528}} In Ise Shinto, the late Ise Shinto, which excluded Buddhism and incorporated Confucianism, was formed in the Edo period by Nobuka Deguchi, a Shinto priest. The essence of Shinto, he wrote, is the way that Japanese people should naturally conduct themselves in their daily lives, the "way of daily use," which is to perform one's duties with honesty and purity of mind. He pointed out that it is a mistake to think that only the rituals at shrines, such as chanting congratulatory prayers and holding ball-shaped sticks, are Shinto.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=533-541}} In addition, he criticized the use of Confucianism and Buddhism for the purpose of learning, arguing that although all religions are ultimately the same, and there are many points of agreement between Shinto and Confucianism, the systems and customs of each country differ, and therefore Japanese people should respect the laws and customs of Japan.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=533-541}} However, he also stated that it is okay to study Confucianism and Buddhism as long as Shinto is placed at the center. He argued that prohibiting Buddhism and Confucianism because of their harmful effects and destroying current customs is against the natural order of things and is different from Shinto.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=533-541}} [[File:Yamazaki_Ansai.jpg|left|thumb|Yaksai Yamazaki, the culmination of Confucian Shinto]] These Confucian theories of Shinto were compiled by {{ill|Yamazaki Ansai|en}}. After making a name for himself as a Confucian scholar, he was taken in by {{ill|Hoshina Masayuki|en}}, Lord of the {{ill|Aizu Domain|en}}, where he came into contact with Masayuki's guest teacher, Yoshikawa Tadashi, and learned Yoshikawa Shinto, leading to the creation of his own Taruka Shinto. The idea was to combine {{ill|Kamiyonanayo|lt=Seven Generations of the Divine Age|en}} with the {{ill|Neo-Confucianism|en}} of the Shuzi school, and to believe that Kunitokotachi-no-Mikoto was the {{ill|Taiji (philosophy)|lt=Taiji|en}}, and that the five gods that arose after him were {{ill|Wuxing (Chinese philosophy)|lt=Five Elements|en}}, and that the last two, {{ill|Izanagi|en}} and {{ill|Izanami|en}}, combined the Five Elements to give birth to the land, gods, and people. The spirit of the god who created the people resides in each person, and the gods and people are in a state of union called "the only way of heaven and man.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=545-550}} He said that Shinto means that people should live according to God, and that people should pray to God to obtain blessings, but that people must be "honest" in order to do so, and that "respect" is the first thing to realize this "honesty.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=545-550}} The relationship between the sovereign and the vassal is not one of rivalry or power, but one of unity, and the sovereign and the vassal have protected the country through their mutual protection.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=545-550}}、He also had a great influence on the later philosophy of the Emperor. After the death of Yaksai Yamazaki, his pupil Shoshinmachi Kimimichi succeeded him, and the Taruka Shinto sect reached its zenith, spreading throughout the country, especially in Edo and Kyoto, widely spreading among nobles, warriors, and priests, and having the greatest influence on the Shinto world.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=551-554}} After the death of Masamichi, his disciple, Masahide Tamaki, succeeded him and organized the single, double, triple, and quadruple mysteries based on the "Mochijusho" written by Masamichi, and worked on the organization of the Taruka Shinto.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=551-554}} Some people, such as Gousai Wakabayashi, criticized this move to make the teachings secret, saying that it would obscure Yaksai's true intentions.{{Sfn|Kokugakuin University Institute of Japanese Culture|1999|pp=437-439|loc=垂加神道（西岡和彦）}} In addition to the Tachibana family Shinto mentioned above, the Hakka Shinto and Tsuchimikado Shinto were organized under the influence of the Taruka Shinto. Yoshimi Yukikazu, who was one of Tamaki Masahide's pupils, wrote a book entitled "Goubu-shosetsu-ben" in which he criticized Ise Shinto and Yoshida Shinto by arguing that the Shinto Goubu-shosetsu was a fake book from the Middle Ages, and also criticized Taruka Shinto, which also used the Goubu-shosetsu as its scriptures.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=551-554}} In fact, after Masahide Tamaki, Taraka Shinto began to stagnate ideologically and surrendered its mainstream position to {{ill|Kokugaku|en}}.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=551-554}} In conjunction with these anti-Buddhist ideological trends, a movement to separate Shinto and Buddhism began to spread in some of the clans that had accepted Confucian Shinto. In the {{ill|Mito Domain|en}}, {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en}} investigated the history of shrines with strong Shinto-Buddhist practices in {{ill|1696|en}} (the 9th year of the {{ill|Genroku|en}}), and organized them in such a way as to wipe out the Buddhist flavor. In addition, Masayuki Hoshina of the Aizu domain carried out a similar reorganization of temples and shrines.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=128}} In addition, {{ill|Ikeda Mitsumasa|en}} of the {{ill|Okayama Domain|en}} promoted the return of priests from the {{ill|Nichiren-shū|en}} {{ill|Fuju-fuse|en}} and Tendai and Shingon sects, reducing the number of temples and encouraging Shinto funerals.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=128}} In {{ill|1647|en}}, {{ill|Matsue Domain|en}}, under the leadership of {{ill|Matsue Domain|en}} lord Matsudaira Naomasa, Buddhist elements were removed from the {{ill|Izumo-taisha|en}}.{{Cite journal|last=Teeuwen|first=Mark|last2=Zhong|first2=Yijiang|date=2017|title=Izumo, Ise, and Modern Shinto|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/90017702|journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies|volume=44|issue=2|pages=325–332|issn=0304-1042}} === Meiji Restoration === In 1869 during the [[Meiji Restoration]] the traditional [[Japanese nobility]] were reformed. , In 1884, the {{ill|Peerage ordinance|ja|華族令}} was passed, and {{ill|Yoshida Yoshiyoshi|ja|吉田良義}} was given the title of {{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}} (Yoshida)|image=File:Yoshida torii sakura 03.jpg|caption=Izumo Taisha, the traditional shrine of the family|parent house=[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]|image caption=[[Yoshida Shrine]], the traditional shrine of the family|alt=[[Yoshida Shrine]], the traditional shrine of the family}} The {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Yoshida clan|ja|吉田家|en|draft:Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family}} ([[:ja:吉田家|吉田家]]) also known as the {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|en|draft:Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family}} ([[:ja:卜部氏|卜部氏]]) were a family of diviners in Japan{{Cite web |title=Yoshida family {{!}} Encyclopedia.com |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/yoshida-family |access-date=2023-03-12 |website=www.encyclopedia.com}}. They were highly influential in the development of Shinto. The historical {{ill|Yoshida Shinto|en}} school of thought which was the norm until the [[Meiji Restoration]] is named after them.{{Cite web|date=2024-03-19|title=Yoshida Shintō {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151532/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9901|access-date=2024-03-19|website=web.archive.org}} They were originally the diviners of the Department of divinities under the Urabe clan name. They served at [[Yoshida Shrine|Yoshida Shrine]], their traditional shrine and namesake.{{Cite web|title=Yoshida family|url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686?d=%2F10.1093%2Foi%2Fauthority.20110803125403686&p=emailAMFctfco71wyE|access-date=2024-03-19|website=Oxford Reference|language=en|doi=10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686?d=/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686&p=emailamfctfco71wye}} == Urabe clan == The Urabe (卜部) clan is a clan whose name is "Urabe." They were one of the ancient ritual aristocrats, specializing in fortune-telling to determine good or bad outcomes. == Contents == 1. Overview 2. Urabe of Izu (伊豆卜部) 3. Urabe of Iki (壱岐卜部) 4. Urabe of Munakata Shrine (Chikuzen Province) 6. Other Urabe 7. Footnote    1. Annotation    2. Reference 8. References == Summary == Urabe is a clan whose occupation was Kameboku (divination by interpreting the cracks formed when a tortoise shell is burned). Different lineages of Urabe clans exist across Japan, with those from Izu (伊豆), Iki (壱岐), and Tsushima (対馬) appointed as officials of the Jingikan (神祇官). The Izu Urabe clan was appointed as vice-ministers (大副 and 少副) of the Jingikan, with 5 people from Izu, 5 from Iki, and 10 from Tsushima appointed to lower-ranking official positions, recognized for their excellence in divination techniques. It is said that Urabe clans not from these three regions are descendants of clans related to Taizan (太占), an ancient form of Japanese divination. == Urabe of Izu == - Surname: From Sukune Urabe (宿禰卜部) to Asaomi Urabe (朝臣卜部) - Ancestor: Hiramaro Urabe (平麻呂卜部) - Descendants include Kaneyoshi Urabe (兼好卜部) - The actual ancestor, Hiramaro Urabe, served in the early Heian period, but details before him are unclear. There are genealogies suggesting Hiramaro was the son of Onakatomi Chijimaro (大中臣千治麿), a grandson of Onakatomi Kiyomaro (大中臣清麿), but these are considered later fabrications. It is theorized they served Mishima Taisha Shrine (三嶋大社) as priests. The surname was changed from Sukune to Asaomi by Yoshida Kanehiro (吉田兼煕) in 1375. The descendants of Hiramaro split into the Yoshida-sha (吉田社) and Hirano-sha (平野社) lineages, serving alternately as Jingi Dai-Vice and Jingi Sho-Vice. == Urabe of Iki == The Iki Urabe clan, associated with Iyoshi Island (伊吉島). Genealogies indicate Maneko no Mikoto (真根子命), a descendant of Raijin no Mikoto (雷神命) and part of Empress Jingu's (神功皇后) retinue, as an ancestor. Despite some claims to Nakatomi (中臣) lineage, discrepancies in genealogical records suggest different origins. == Urabe of Tsushima == The Tsushima Urabe clan, associated with the Tsushima Prefecture (対馬府) ruling family. Ancestral origins vary across historical sources, including deities like Takehiradori no Mikoto (建比良鳥命) and Raidaijin no Mikoto (雷大臣命). == Urabe Serving Shrines == - **Kashima Shrine (鹿嶋神宮) in Hitachi Province:** Served from ancient times, involved in divination. - **Katsuragi Hitotoshi Shrine (葛城一言主神社) in Yamato Province:** Ancestor served as a priest. - **Munakata Shrine (宗像大社) in Chikuzen Province:** Ancestors served, later becoming vassals of the Kuroda clan (黒田氏). == Other Urabe == Beyond the mentioned, the Urabe surname appears in ancient and Nara period records across regions like Mutsu (陸奥), Shimousa (下総), Suruga (駿河), Omi (近江), and Inaba (因幡) Provinces. == History == {{Main|en:History of Shinto}} The origins of the Yoshida family date back to the [[Heian period]] or earlier.
