However, the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏|en||simple|User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan}} who also has roots in this region, and when they took over control of priestly duties from the Ō clan, they also instituted Takemikazuchi as the Nakatomi clan's [[ujigami]] (clan deity). Or so this is the observation by {{Interlanguage link multi|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup}} {{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}} was the first person to have the name Yoshida, taken from [[Yoshida Shrine]] which he ran. The Yoshida faimly grew immensely powerful later. == Summary == Urabe is a clan whose occupation was Kameboku (divination by interpreting the cracks formed when a tortoise shell is burned). Different lineages of Urabe clans exist across Japan, with those from Izu (伊豆), Iki (壱岐), and Tsushima (対馬) appointed as officials of the Jingikan (神祇官). The Izu Urabe clan was appointed as vice-ministers (大副 and 少副) of the Jingikan, with 5 people from Izu, 5 from Iki, and 10 from Tsushima appointed to lower-ranking official positions, recognized for their excellence in divination techniques. It is said that Urabe clans not from these three regions are descendants of clans related to Taizan (太占), an ancient form of Japanese divination. == Urabe of Izu == - Surname: From Sukune Urabe (宿禰卜部) to Asaomi Urabe (朝臣卜部) - Ancestor: Hiramaro Urabe (平麻呂卜部) - Descendants include Kaneyoshi Urabe (兼好卜部) - The actual ancestor, Hiramaro Urabe, served in the early Heian period, but details before him are unclear. There are genealogies suggesting Hiramaro was the son of Onakatomi Chijimaro (大中臣千治麿), a grandson of Onakatomi Kiyomaro (大中臣清麿), but these are considered later fabrications. It is theorized they served Mishima Taisha Shrine (三嶋大社) as priests. The surname was changed from Sukune to Asaomi by Yoshida Kanehiro (吉田兼煕) in 1375. The descendants of Hiramaro split into the Yoshida-sha (吉田社) and Hirano-sha (平野社) lineages, serving alternately as Jingi Dai-Vice and Jingi Sho-Vice. == Urabe of Iki == The Iki Urabe clan, associated with Iyoshi Island (伊吉島). Genealogies indicate Maneko no Mikoto (真根子命), a descendant of Raijin no Mikoto (雷神命) and part of Empress Jingu's (神功皇后) retinue, as an ancestor. Despite some claims to Nakatomi (中臣) lineage, discrepancies in genealogical records suggest different origins.{{Cite journal|last=Kory|first=Stephan N.|date=2015|title=From Deer Bones to Turtle Shells: The State Ritualization of Pyro-Plastromancy during the Nara-Heian Transition|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/43686907|journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies|volume=42|issue=2|pages=339–380|issn=0304-1042}} == Urabe of Tsushima == The Tsushima Urabe clan, associated with the Tsushima Prefecture (対馬府) ruling family. Ancestral origins vary across historical sources, including deities like Takehiradori no Mikoto (建比良鳥命) and Raidaijin no Mikoto (雷大臣命).{{Cite journal|last=Grapard|first=Allan G.|date=1992|title=The Shinto of Yoshida Kanetomo|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2385357|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=47|issue=1|pages=27–58|doi=10.2307/2385357|issn=0027-0741}}{{Cite web|title=Cultural Properties {{!}} Japan Heritage Border Islands of Iki, Tsushima and Goto. A Bridge from Ancient Times.|url=https://kokkyonoshima.com/eng/places/bunkazai|access-date=2024-04-03|website=Cultural Properties {{!}} Japan Heritage Border Islands of Iki, Tsushima and Goto. A Bridge from Ancient Times.}}{{Cite web|title=Things to do in Tsushima in December|url=https://wanderlog.com/geoInMonth/506/12/tsushima-in-december|access-date=2024-04-03|website=Wanderlog}}{{Cite web|date=2024-03-19|title=Kiboku {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151536/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=8574|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}}https://web.archive.org/web/20240403160613/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9920 == Shrines served by the Urabe == - {{ill|Kashima-jingū|ja|鹿嶋神宮}} (鹿嶋神宮) in Hitachi Province: Served from ancient times, involved in divination. - {{ill|Katsuragi Hitotoshi Shrine|ja|葛城一言主神社}} (葛城一言主神社) in Yamato Province: Ancestor served as a priest. - {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社}} (宗像大社) in Chikuzen Province: Ancestors served, later becoming vassals of the {{ill|Kuroda clan|ja|黒田氏}} (黒田氏). == Other Urabe == Beyond the mentioned, the Urabe surname appears in ancient and Nara period records across regions like Mutsu (陸奥), Shimousa (下総), Suruga (駿河), Omi (近江), and Inaba (因幡) Provinces. == Yoshida family == The Yoshida Family is a family of court nobles and kazoku descended from the Urabe Clan. As court nobles, they were classified as a {{ill|Half House|ja|半家 (公家)}}, and as {{ill|Kazoku|ja|華族}}, their rank was that of a [[viscount]]. == Yoshida family history == The family's founder, Yoshida Kaneoki, known for transferring his residence's land in Kyoto's Muromachi Koji to Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, named the family "Yoshida" after the Yoshida Shrine, where he served. Kaneoki was the first from the Urabe Clan to become a high-ranking official, serving as Jingi-no-Daifu (Deputy of the Department of Worship) and Jiju (Chamberlain). == Urabe Kanekata (fl. 1274 - 1301) == The Yoshida family (吉田家) originally bore the surname Urabe (卜部), and their lineage traditionally held the position of Jingi Daifu (神祇大副), the vice-official of the [[Department of Divinities]], specializing in divination by turtle shell throughout generations. In the medieval period, Urabe Kanekata (卜部兼方) was known for his expertise in Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) studies, earning the title "The Nihon Shoki Family."{{Cite web|date=2024-03-25|title=Urabe Kanekata {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240325211917/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9861|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}} == Yoshida Kanetomo (吉田 兼倶, 1435–1511) == The 5th generation, Kanetomo, founded a unique form of Shinto, expanding his influence by gaining Emperor Gomizunoo as a follower, despite fierce opposition from the existing priesthood of the Ise Shrine lineage. He self-proclaimed the new title of "Jingi Kanrei Chojou" (Supreme Leader of the Department of Worship), later ousting the Shirakawa family, who were Jingi Haku (heads of the Department of Worship), and expanding his control over shrines nationwide. [[File:吉田兼倶肖像画.jpg|thumb|Yoshida Kanetomo]] During the {{ill|Ōnin|en}} reign, the {{ill|Ōnin War|en}} broke out and Kyoto was burnt to the ground, affecting many temples and shrines, and causing the abortion of imperial court rituals such as the {{ill|Daijosai|en}} and the coronation ceremony. One of the priests who was shocked by the upheaval was {{ill|Yoshida Kanetomo|en}}. Kanetomo, who was so upset that he lost his own {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}} to the war, as well as more than a dozen residents of the area around the shrine.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=182}} However, the loss of many ancient manuscripts due to the war led to the formation of a new Shinto theory called {{ill|Yoshida Shintō|en}}.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=234}}[[File:Yoshida_shrine_funeral_hall.jpg|left|thumb|{{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}} in {{ill|Sakyō-ku, Kyoto|lt=Sakyo-ku|en}} {{ill|Kyoto|Kyoto City|en}}]]Kanetomo authored texts such as "Shintō Daimi" (神道大意) and "Yuiitsu Shintō Meihō Yōshū" (唯一神道名法要集), synthesizing medieval Shinto thought and incorporating discourses from various religions to propose Yoshida Shinto. In this doctrine, he classified Shinto into three categories: "Honjaku Engi Shintō" (本迹縁起神道), "Ryōbu Shūgō Shintō" (両部習合神道), and "Genpon Shūgen Shintō" (元本宗源神道), declaring the "Genpon Shūgen Shintō" passed down in his family as the legitimate Shinto since the nation's founding. He defined gods as the "spiritual ancestors of heaven and earth" and the way as the "origin of all actions."{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=236-237}} He also strongly advocated the root-branch-fruit theory, positioning Shinto as the root, [[Confucianism]] as its branches manifesting in [[China]], and [[Buddhism]] as the fruit blossoming in India, asserting that Shinto encapsulates the essence of all religions.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=113}} Furthermore, Kanetomo argued that Shinto has three aspects: "substance" (体), "form" (相), and "function" (用), governing various phenomena like the sun and moon, cold and heat, and nature. Ultimately, he envisioned a pantheistic view where gods reside within all aspects of the universe, pervading the cosmos.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=237-238}} Kanetomo also established numerous rituals. He constructed the Dai Ōtomiya Saijō at the [[Yoshida Shrine]] precincts, proclaiming it as the foundation for rituals since Emperor Jimmu, serving as the main sanctuary for inner and outer shrines, eight god temples, and over three thousand official shrines nationwide.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=235-236}} Influenced by Esoteric Buddhism, he devised {{ill|Homa (ritual)|lt=Homa|en}} rituals involving a fire in an octagonal platform centered around a stove, contributing to the formation of three major rituals alongside "Jūhachido Shintō Gyoji" and "Sōgen Shintō Gyoji."{{Cite web|title=吉田神道行事壇|url=http://museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/exhibition/detail/id=4|access-date=2021-03-02|publisher=國學院大學博物館}} These teachings were expounded by the "Three Nerves" of the Tengen Shinhen Shinmyou Sutra, the Local Shinto Shinmyou Sutra, and the Jingen Shinryoku Shinmyou Sutra.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=236}} These sutras were said to be the teachings of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame-no-Koyane|en}}, but these three sutras are fictitious and there is no evidence that they were ever produced.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=239}} Kanetomo forged sutras similar to these by posing as the authors, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en}}, to create his own sutras.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=239-240}} The history of the sanctuary was also created by Kanetomo himself.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=240}} Yoshida Shinto established the ritual of enshrining humans as gods. Traditionally, Shinto saw death as [[Kegare|impure]] and seldom involved in funeral rites, with human enshrinement limited to pacifying vengeful spirits or celestial deity worship. However, Yoshida Shinto, viewing a close relationship between humans and gods, actively conducted funerary rites, with Kanetomo establishing the Shinryūsha as a spiritual shrine over the deceased's remains.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=186-187}} Yoshida Shinto is the first Shinto theory to have its own doctrines, scriptures, and rituals independent of Buddhism, while integrating various religious discourses in a cross-border manner.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=243}}、The Shinto scholar {{ill|Okada Chuangji|ja|岡田莊司}} described the establishment of Yoshida Shinto as "a turning point in the history of Shinto.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=17}}、The historian {{ill|Toshio Kuroda|en}} argues that the establishment of Yoshida Shinto was the establishment of Shinto{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=16}} It is considered by several researchers to be a turning point in the history of Shinto. == Hino Tomiko (日野 富子, 1440 – June 30, 1496) == Although Yoshida Shinto was an emerging force, it rapidly rose to prominence, perhaps due to the social unrest of the age of war, and was widely accepted, especially by the upper classes, as it received the support of {{ill|Hino Tomiko|en}} in the construction of the Omoto Shrine, and even received the imperial approval of the Omoto Shrine in {{ill|1473|en}} ({{ill|Bunmei|en}}5).{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=235}}、The center of the Shinto world in modern times.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=244}} On the other hand, it received strong protests from priests of [[Ise Grand Shrine]].{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=243}} == {{ill|Yoshida Kanemi|ja|吉田兼見|fa|یوشیدا کانه‌می}} (1535-1610) == As mentioned above, Yoshida Shinto, which established Shinto funeral rites, became involved in the construction of shrines that enshrined warring feudal lords as gods in the Warring States period, and Kanemi Yoshida was involved in the construction of {{ill|Toyokuni Shrine (Kyoto)|lt=Toyokuni Shrine|en}}, which enshrined {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en}} as a god. Shinryuin Bonshun of the Yoshida family taught Shinto to {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en}}, and according to his will, conducted a Shinto funeral service after Ieyasu's death.{{Cite web|last=鎌田純一|date=2017-10-19|title=梵舜|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%A2%B5%E8%88%9C-135079|access-date=2021-07-06|publisher=コトバンク（日本大百科全書）}}(However, {{ill|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|en}} became the {{ill|Sanno Shinto|en}} style after {{ill|Tenkai|en}} won the debate). When the era of warfare ended and the Edo period began, the administration of shrines was reorganized. The shogunate first relieved each shrine of its current territory and granted it the privilege of "not entering into the custody of the guardian. However, what was granted was the right to make profits from the shrines, and the ownership of the land belonged to the shogunate.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=191}} The {{ill|Shogun|lt=Shogunate|en}} also established the {{ill|Jisha-bugyō|en}} as a position reporting directly to the shogun, and placed it at the head of the three magistrates, surpassing the {{ill|Machi-bugyō|lt=Town Magistrate|en}} and {{ill|Kanjō-bugyō|lt=Account Magistrate|en}} under the jurisdiction of the {{ill|Rōjū|lt=Rōchū|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=191-192}} In addition, a Shinto department under the jurisdiction of the temple and shrine magistrates was established to study the truths of Shinto and the rituals of rituals and to respond to the advice of the temple and shrine magistrates.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=192}} On the other hand, individual magistrates were assigned to specific shrines, such as {{ill|Yamada bugyō|en}}, who was in charge of Ise Shrine, and Nikko bugyō, who was in charge of {{ill|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|lt=Nikko Tōshō-gū|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=198}} By the 9th generation, {{ill|Yoshida Kanemi|ja|吉田兼見|fa|یوشیدا کانه‌می}}, with the support of [[Oda Nobunaga]], the family achieved the court noble status{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Yoshida Kanemi {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207101954/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9845|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}}. Serving as a family ritualist to Konoe Sakihisa and forming a deep friendship with Akechi Mitsuhide, Kanemi's diary, "Kanjokyoki," became an essential resource for the study of the Azuchi-Momoyama period. The Yoshida family's dominance in priesthood was solidified in the [[Edo period]], particularly with the "Various Shrine's Negi and Kannushi Laws" in 1665. In {{ill|1665|en}} (the fifth year of the {{ill|Kanbun (era)|lt=Kanbun|en}}), the shogunate issued the Priest Law for Priests of Various Shrines, which stated that ordinary {{ill|Kannushi|lt=Priests|en}} without rank must obtain a Shinto license issued by the Yoshida family before they can wear a hunting robe or crown, giving the Yoshida family control over almost all priests.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=192-196}} However, it was approved that those families that had been conferred ranks by the Imperial Court through transmission, such as [[Ise Grand Shrine]], {{ill|Kamo Shrine|en}}, {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}, {{ill|Usa Jingū|en}}, {{ill|Izumo-taisha|en}}, and {{ill|Fushimi Inari-taisha|en}}, would continue to use the same methods as before, without the Yoshida family.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=193}} In addition, the law stipulates penalties for neglect of duties by priests, prohibition of sales and purchases of shrine property, and the obligation to repair shrine buildings. The Shogunate also financially supported the partial revival of the imperial rituals that had been suspended due to warfare. After 222 years of interruptions since {{ill|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|en}}, the Dai-namesai was revived in the reign of {{ill|Emperor Higashiyama|en}}, and became a regular event since {{ill|Emperor Sakuramachi|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} The {{ill|Niiname-no-Matsuri|en}} was also revived in {{ill|1688|en}} (the first year of {{ill|Genroku|en}}), the year after the restoration of the Dai-namesai.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} In {{ill|1744|en}} (the first year of {{ill|Enkyō (Edo period)|Enkyo|en}}), some of the votive offerings were also revived, including those to {{ill|Twenty-Two Shrines|en}} and to Usa Hachiman Shrine and {{ill|Kashii-gū|lt=Kashii Shrine|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} The Imperial Court's dispatch of imperial envoys on the occasion of the Shinnamesai festival was revived in {{ill|1647|en}} (the fourth year of the {{ill|Shōhō|lt=Shohoho|en}}) by the special order of {{ill|Emperor Go-Kōmyō|en}}. The ceremonial relocation of the Ise Jingu Shrine was also suspended, but was rebuilt during the {{ill|Azuchi-Momoyama period|lt2=Orifuji administration|en}} thanks to the efforts of Seisun and Shuyou of Keikoin. The {{ill|Department of Divinities|en}}, which was destroyed by fire during the war, was replaced by the eight temples at the Yoshida Shrine, and the Divinities themselves were not rebuilt.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=190-191}} == Later Edo period == The family heads were known as Jingi Kanrei Chojou, holding the highest position of Jingi-no-Daifu at the rank of Shonii (Senior Second Rank). During the Edo period, the family's stipend was 760 koku. A branch family, the Hagiwara family, emerged in the early Edo period. In Yoshida Shinto, a merchant named {{ill|Yoshikawa Tadashi|ja|吉川惟足}} was initiated into the Yoshida family and received the "Shinto Doutou" (神道同統) from the head of the Yoshida family, Hagiwara Kenju (萩原兼従), becoming the official successor. He formed Yoshikawa Shinto by removing Buddhist discourse from Yoshida Shinto and incorporating more Confucian teachings. Its ideology first posits that Shinto is the origin of all laws, and that [[Kuni-no-Tokotachi|Kunitokotachi]] (国常立尊) is the sovereign of the world. It argues that the world and humans were created through "{{ill|Li_(neo-Confucianism)|ja|理|lt=Li}}" (理), identical to the gods, and that "{{ill|Li_(neo-Confucianism)|ja|理|lt=Li}}" inherently exists within the human body. Thus, originally humans and gods were one, but the divine wisdom becomes clouded by the impurities of the human heart. Therefore, it is necessary to return to one's original state through "caution" (つつしみ). As concrete methods, it advocated purification rituals to cleanse both internally and externally, expressing sincerity through festival rites, and praying to the gods. Moreover, it stated that the five cardinal relationships in Confucianism are the mission given by the gods to humans, especially emphasizing the importance of the relationship between lord and retainer.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=522-528}}{{Cite web|date=2023-03-14|title=Yoshikawa Shintō {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230314175907/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9902|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}} == Meiji Restoration == In 1869 (Meiji 2), during the [[Meiji Restoration]] the traditional [[Japanese nobility]] were reformed. The Yoshida family were elevated to the kazoku peerage, and in 1884 (Meiji 17), upon the enactment of the {{ill|Peerage ordinance|ja|華族令}}, {{ill|Yoshida Yoshiyoshi|lt=Yoshiyoshi|ja|吉田良義}} was bestowed the title of [[viscount]]. The residence of the Yoshida baronial family was located in Ichigaya Nakanocho, Ushigome Ward, Tokyo. {{ill|Yoshida Kiyonari|en}} was another member who was also awarded the title of [[viscount]].{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PcG1AQAAQBAJ|title=The Satsuma Students in Britain: Japan's Early Search for the essence of the {{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}} (Yoshida)|image=File:Yoshida torii sakura 03.jpg|caption=Izumo Taisha, the traditional shrine of the family|parent house=[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]|image caption=[[Yoshida Shrine]], the traditional shrine of the family|alt=[[Yoshida Shrine]], the traditional shrine of the family}} The {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|en|draft:Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family}} ([[:ja:卜部氏|卜部氏]]) were a family of diviners in Japan{{Cite web |title=Yoshida family {{!}} Encyclopedia.com |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/yoshida-family |access-date=2023-03-12 |website=www.encyclopedia.com}}.{{rp|35}}. Their [[cadet branch]] the Yoshida family is one of the most historically influential shinto priest families. They were highly influential in the development of Shinto. The historical {{ill|Yoshida Shinto|en}} school of thought which was the norm until the [[Meiji Restoration]] is named after them.{{Cite web|date=2024-03-19|title=Yoshida Shintō {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151532/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9901|access-date=2024-03-19|website=web.archive.org}} They were originally the diviners of the Department of divinities under the Urabe clan name.{{Cite web|title=Jingidoke|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151308/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9910|access-date=2024-03-19|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} They served at [[Yoshida Shrine|Yoshida Shrine]], their traditional shrine and namesake.{{Cite web|title=Yoshida family|url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686?d=%2F10.1093%2Foi%2Fauthority.20110803125403686&p=emailAMFctfco71wyE|access-date=2024-03-19|website=Oxford Reference|language=en|doi=10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686?d=/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686&p=emailamfctfco71wye}} The Yoshida Family is a family of court nobles and kazoku descended from the Urabe Clan. As court nobles, they were classified as a {{ill|Half House|ja|半家 (公家)}}, and as {{ill|Kazoku|ja|華族}}, their rank was that of a [[viscount]]. == History == {{Main|en:History of Shinto}} The origins of the Yoshida family date back to the [[Heian period]] or earlier. They claimed descent from {{ill|Ame no Koyane|en}}.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_Q81DQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto: A History|last=Hardacre|first=Helen|date=2017|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-062171-1|language=en}}{{rp|25-26}} It is believed that originally the Urabe clan was a low clan subordinate to the {{ill|Nakatomi Or so this is the observation by {{Interlanguage link multi|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup}} {{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}} was the first person to have the name Yoshida, taken from [[Yoshida Shrine]] which he ran. The Yoshida faimly grew immensely powerful later. == Summary == Urabe is a clan whose occupation was Kameboku (divination by interpreting the cracks formed when a tortoise shell is burned). Different lineages of Urabe clans exist across Japan, with those from Izu (伊豆), Iki (壱岐), and Tsushima (対馬) appointed as officials of the Jingikan (神祇官). The Izu Urabe clan was appointed as vice-ministers (大副 and 少副) of the Jingikan, with 5 people from Izu, 5 from Iki, and 10 from Tsushima appointed to lower-ranking official positions, recognized for their excellence in divination techniques. It is said that Urabe clans not from these three regions are descendants of clans related to Taizan (太占), an ancient form of Japanese divination. == Urabe of Izu == - Surname: From Sukune Urabe (宿禰卜部) to Asaomi Urabe (朝臣卜部) - Ancestor: Hiramaro Urabe (平麻呂卜部) - Descendants include Kaneyoshi Urabe (兼好卜部) - The actual ancestor, Hiramaro Urabe, served in the early Heian period, but details before him are unclear. There are genealogies suggesting Hiramaro was the son of Onakatomi Chijimaro (大中臣千治麿), a grandson of Onakatomi Kiyomaro (大中臣清麿), but these are considered later fabrications. It is theorized they served Mishima Taisha Shrine (三嶋大社) as priests. The surname was changed from Sukune to Asaomi by Yoshida Kanehiro (吉田兼煕) in 1375. The descendants of Hiramaro split into the Yoshida-sha (吉田社) and Hirano-sha (平野社) lineages, serving alternately as Jingi Dai-Vice and Jingi Sho-Vice. == Urabe of Iki == The Iki Urabe clan, associated with Iyoshi Island (伊吉島). Genealogies indicate Maneko no Mikoto (真根子命), a descendant of Raijin no Mikoto (雷神命) and part of Empress Jingu's (神功皇后) retinue, as an ancestor. Despite some claims to Nakatomi (中臣) lineage, discrepancies in genealogical records suggest different origins.{{Cite journal|last=Kory|first=Stephan N.|date=2015|title=From Deer Bones to Turtle Shells: The State Ritualization of Pyro-Plastromancy during the Nara-Heian Transition|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/43686907|journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies|volume=42|issue=2|pages=339–380|issn=0304-1042}} == Urabe of Tsushima == The Tsushima Urabe clan, associated with the Tsushima Prefecture (対馬府) ruling family. Ancestral origins vary across historical sources, including deities like Takehiradori no Mikoto (建比良鳥命) and Raidaijin no Mikoto (雷大臣命).{{Cite journal|last=Grapard|first=Allan G.|date=1992|title=The Shinto of Yoshida Kanetomo|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2385357|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=47|issue=1|pages=27–58|doi=10.2307/2385357|issn=0027-0741}}{{Cite web|title=Cultural Properties {{!}} Japan Heritage Border Islands of Iki, Tsushima and Goto. A Bridge from Ancient Times.|url=https://kokkyonoshima.com/eng/places/bunkazai|access-date=2024-04-03|website=Cultural Properties {{!}} Japan Heritage Border Islands of Iki, Tsushima and Goto. A Bridge from Ancient Times.}}{{Cite web|title=Things to do in Tsushima in December|url=https://wanderlog.com/geoInMonth/506/12/tsushima-in-december|access-date=2024-04-03|website=Wanderlog}}{{Cite web|date=2024-03-19|title=Kiboku {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151536/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=8574|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}}https://web.archive.org/web/20240403160613/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9920 == Shrines served by the Urabe == - {{ill|Kashima-jingū|ja|鹿嶋神宮}} (鹿嶋神宮) in Hitachi Province: Served from ancient times, involved in divination. - {{ill|Katsuragi Hitotoshi Shrine|ja|葛城一言主神社}} (葛城一言主神社) in Yamato Province: Ancestor served as a priest. - {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社}} (宗像大社) in Chikuzen Province: Ancestors served, later becoming vassals of the {{ill|Kuroda clan|ja|黒田氏}} (黒田氏). == Other Urabe == Beyond the mentioned, the Urabe surname appears in ancient and Nara period records across regions like Mutsu (陸奥), Shimousa (下総), Suruga (駿河), Omi (近江), and Inaba (因幡) Provinces. == Yoshida family == The Yoshida Family is a family of court nobles and kazoku descended from the Urabe Clan. As court nobles, they were classified as a {{ill|Half House|ja|半家 (公家)}}, and as {{ill|Kazoku|ja|華族}}, their rank was that of a [[viscount]]. == Yoshida family history == The family's founder, Yoshida Kaneoki, known for transferring his residence's land in Kyoto's Muromachi Koji to Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, named the family "Yoshida" after the [[Yoshida Shrine]], where he served. Kaneoki was the first from the Urabe Clan to become a high-ranking official, serving as Jingi-no-Daifu (Deputy of the [[Department of Divinities]]) and Jiju (Chamberlain). == Urabe Kanekata (fl. 1274 - 1301) == The Yoshida family (吉田家) originally bore the surname Urabe (卜部), and their lineage traditionally held the position of Jingi Daifu (神祇大副), the vice-official of the [[Department of Divinities]], specializing in divination by turtle shell throughout generations. In the medieval period, Urabe Kanekata (卜部兼方) was known for his expertise in Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) studies, earning the title "The Nihon Shoki Family."{{Cite web|date=2024-03-25|title=Urabe Kanekata {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240325211917/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9861|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}} == Yoshida Kanetomo (吉田 兼倶, 1435–1511) == The 5th generation, Kanetomo, founded a unique form of Shinto, expanding his influence by gaining Emperor Gomizunoo as a follower, despite fierce opposition from the existing priesthood of the Ise Shrine lineage. He self-proclaimed the new title of "Jingi Kanrei Chojou" (Supreme Leader of the Department of Worship), later ousting the Shirakawa family, who were Jingi Haku (heads of the Department of Worship), and expanding his control over shrines nationwide. [[File:吉田兼倶肖像画.jpg|thumb|Yoshida Kanetomo]] During the {{ill|Ōnin|en}} reign, the {{ill|Ōnin War|en}} broke out and Kyoto was burnt to the ground, affecting many temples and shrines, and causing the abortion of imperial court rituals such as the {{ill|Daijosai|en}} and the coronation ceremony. One of the priests who was shocked by the upheaval was {{ill|Yoshida Kanetomo|en}}. Kanetomo, who was so upset that he lost his own {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}} to the war, as well as more than a dozen residents of the area around the shrine.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=182}} However, the loss of many ancient manuscripts due to the war led to the formation of a new Shinto theory called {{ill|Yoshida Shintō|en}}.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=234}}[[File:Yoshida_shrine_funeral_hall.jpg|left|thumb|{{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}} in {{ill|Sakyō-ku, Kyoto|lt=Sakyo-ku|en}} {{ill|Kyoto|Kyoto City|en}}]]Kanetomo authored texts such as "Shintō Daimi" (神道大意) and "Yuiitsu Shintō Meihō Yōshū" (唯一神道名法要集), synthesizing medieval Shinto thought and incorporating discourses from various religions to propose Yoshida Shinto. In this doctrine, he classified Shinto into three categories: "Honjaku Engi Shintō" (本迹縁起神道), "Ryōbu Shūgō Shintō" (両部習合神道), and "Genpon Shūgen Shintō" (元本宗源神道), declaring the "Genpon Shūgen Shintō" passed down in his family as the legitimate Shinto since the nation's founding. He defined gods as the "spiritual ancestors of heaven and earth" and the way as the "origin of all actions."{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=236-237}} He also strongly advocated the root-branch-fruit theory, positioning Shinto as the root, [[Confucianism]] as its branches manifesting in [[China]], and [[Buddhism]] as the fruit blossoming in India, asserting that Shinto encapsulates the essence of all religions.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=113}} Furthermore, Kanetomo argued that Shinto has three aspects: "substance" (体), "form" (相), and "function" (用), governing various phenomena like the sun and moon, cold and heat, and nature. Ultimately, he envisioned a pantheistic view where gods reside within all aspects of the universe, pervading the cosmos.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=237-238}} Kanetomo also established numerous rituals. He constructed the Dai Ōtomiya Saijō at the [[Yoshida Shrine]] precincts, proclaiming it as the foundation for rituals since Emperor Jimmu, serving as the main sanctuary for inner and outer shrines, eight god temples, and over three thousand official shrines nationwide.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=235-236}} Influenced by Esoteric Buddhism, he devised {{ill|Homa (ritual)|lt=Homa|en}} rituals involving a fire in an octagonal platform centered around a stove, contributing to the formation of three major rituals alongside "Jūhachido Shintō Gyoji" and "Sōgen Shintō Gyoji."{{Cite web|title=吉田神道行事壇|url=http://museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/exhibition/detail/id=4|access-date=2021-03-02|publisher=國學院大學博物館}} These teachings were expounded by the "Three Nerves" of the Tengen Shinhen Shinmyou Sutra, the Local Shinto Shinmyou Sutra, and the Jingen Shinryoku Shinmyou Sutra.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=236}} These sutras were said to be the teachings of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame-no-Koyane|en}}, but these three sutras are fictitious and there is no evidence that they were ever produced.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=239}} Kanetomo forged sutras similar to these by posing as the authors, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en}}, to create his own sutras.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=239-240}} The history of the sanctuary was also created by Kanetomo himself.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=240}} Yoshida Shinto established the ritual of enshrining humans as gods. Traditionally, Shinto saw death as [[Kegare|impure]] and seldom involved in funeral rites, with human enshrinement limited to pacifying vengeful spirits or celestial deity worship. However, Yoshida Shinto, viewing a close relationship between humans and gods, actively conducted funerary rites, with Kanetomo establishing the Shinryūsha as a spiritual shrine over the deceased's remains.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=186-187}} Yoshida Shinto is the first Shinto theory to have its own doctrines, scriptures, and rituals independent of Buddhism, while integrating various religious discourses in a cross-border manner.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=243}}、The Shinto scholar {{ill|Okada Chuangji|ja|岡田莊司}} described the establishment of Yoshida Shinto as "a turning point in the history of Shinto.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=17}}、The historian {{ill|Toshio Kuroda|en}} argues that the establishment of Yoshida Shinto was the establishment of Shinto{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=16}} It is considered by several researchers to be a turning point in the history of Shinto. == Hino Tomiko (日野 富子, 1440 – June 30, 1496) == Although Yoshida Shinto was an emerging force, it rapidly rose to prominence, perhaps due to the social unrest of the age of war, and was widely accepted, especially by the upper classes, as it received the support of {{ill|Hino Tomiko|en}} in the construction of the Omoto Shrine, and even received the imperial approval of the Omoto Shrine in {{ill|1473|en}} ({{ill|Bunmei|en}}5).{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=235}}、The center of the Shinto world in modern times.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=244}} On the other hand, it received strong protests from priests of [[Ise Grand Shrine]].{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=243}} == {{ill|Yoshida Kanemi|ja|吉田兼見|fa|یوشیدا کانه‌می}} (1535-1610) == As mentioned above, Yoshida Shinto, which established Shinto funeral rites, became involved in the construction of shrines that enshrined warring feudal lords as gods in the Warring States period, and Kanemi Yoshida was involved in the construction of {{ill|Toyokuni Shrine (Kyoto)|lt=Toyokuni Shrine|en}}, which enshrined {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en}} as a god. Shinryuin Bonshun of the Yoshida family taught Shinto to {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en}}, and according to his will, conducted a Shinto funeral service after Ieyasu's death.{{Cite web|last=鎌田純一|date=2017-10-19|title=梵舜|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%A2%B5%E8%88%9C-135079|access-date=2021-07-06|publisher=コトバンク（日本大百科全書）}}(However, {{ill|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|en}} became the {{ill|Sanno Shinto|en}} style after {{ill|Tenkai|en}} won the debate). When the era of warfare ended and the Edo period began, the administration of shrines was reorganized. The shogunate first relieved each shrine of its current territory and granted it the privilege of "not entering into the custody of the guardian. However, what was granted was the right to make profits from the shrines, and the ownership of the land belonged to the shogunate.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=191}} The {{ill|Shogun|lt=Shogunate|en}} also established the {{ill|Jisha-bugyō|en}} as a position reporting directly to the shogun, and placed it at the head of the three magistrates, surpassing the {{ill|Machi-bugyō|lt=Town Magistrate|en}} and {{ill|Kanjō-bugyō|lt=Account Magistrate|en}} under the jurisdiction of the {{ill|Rōjū|lt=Rōchū|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=191-192}} In addition, a Shinto department under the jurisdiction of the temple and shrine magistrates was established to study the truths of Shinto and the rituals of rituals and to respond to the advice of the temple and shrine magistrates.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=192}} On the other hand, individual magistrates were assigned to specific shrines, such as {{ill|Yamada bugyō|en}}, who was in charge of Ise Shrine, and Nikko bugyō, who was in charge of {{ill|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|lt=Nikko Tōshō-gū|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=198}} By the 9th generation, {{ill|Yoshida Kanemi|ja|吉田兼見|fa|یوشیدا کانه‌می}}, with the support of [[Oda Nobunaga]], the family achieved the court noble status{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Yoshida Kanemi {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207101954/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9845|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}}. Serving as a family ritualist to Konoe Sakihisa and forming a deep friendship with Akechi Mitsuhide, Kanemi's diary, "Kanjokyoki," became an essential resource for the study of the Azuchi-Momoyama period. The Yoshida family's dominance in priesthood was solidified in the [[Edo period]], particularly with the "Various Shrine's Negi and Kannushi Laws" in 1665. In {{ill|1665|en}} (the fifth year of the {{ill|Kanbun (era)|lt=Kanbun|en}}), the shogunate issued the Priest Law for Priests of Various Shrines, which stated that ordinary {{ill|Kannushi|lt=Priests|en}} without rank must obtain a Shinto license issued by the Yoshida family before they can wear a hunting robe or crown, giving the Yoshida family control over almost all priests.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=192-196}} However, it was approved that those families that had been conferred ranks by the Imperial Court through transmission, such as [[Ise Grand Shrine]], {{ill|Kamo Shrine|en}}, {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}, {{ill|Usa Jingū|en}}, {{ill|Izumo-taisha|en}}, and {{ill|Fushimi Inari-taisha|en}}, would continue to use the same methods as before, without the Yoshida family.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=193}} In addition, the law stipulates penalties for neglect of duties by priests, prohibition of sales and purchases of shrine property, and the obligation to repair shrine buildings. The Shogunate also financially supported the partial revival of the imperial rituals that had been suspended due to warfare. After 222 years of interruptions since {{ill|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|en}}, the Dai-namesai was revived in the reign of {{ill|Emperor Higashiyama|en}}, and became a regular event since {{ill|Emperor Sakuramachi|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} The {{ill|Niiname-no-Matsuri|en}} was also revived in {{ill|1688|en}} (the first year of {{ill|Genroku|en}}), the year after the restoration of the Dai-namesai.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} In {{ill|1744|en}} (the first year of {{ill|Enkyō (Edo period)|Enkyo|en}}), some of the votive offerings were also revived, including those to {{ill|Twenty-Two Shrines|en}} and to Usa Hachiman Shrine and {{ill|Kashii-gū|lt=Kashii Shrine|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} The Imperial Court's dispatch of imperial envoys on the occasion of the Shinnamesai festival was revived in {{ill|1647|en}} (the fourth year of the {{ill|Shōhō|lt=Shohoho|en}}) by the special order of {{ill|Emperor Go-Kōmyō|en}}. The ceremonial relocation of the Ise Jingu Shrine was also suspended, but was rebuilt during the {{ill|Azuchi-Momoyama period|lt2=Orifuji administration|en}} thanks to the efforts of Seisun and Shuyou of Keikoin. The {{ill|Department of Divinities|en}}, which was destroyed by fire during the war, was replaced by the eight temples at the Yoshida Shrine, and the Divinities themselves were not rebuilt.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=190-191}} == Later Edo period == The family heads were known as Jingi Kanrei Chojou, holding the highest position of Jingi-no-Daifu at the rank of Shonii (Senior Second Rank). During the Edo period, the family's stipend was 760 koku. A branch family, the Hagiwara family, emerged in the early Edo period. In Yoshida Shinto, a merchant named {{ill|Yoshikawa Tadashi|ja|吉川惟足}} was initiated into the Yoshida family and received the "Shinto Doutou" (神道同統) from the head of the Yoshida family, Hagiwara Kenju (萩原兼従), becoming the official successor. He formed Yoshikawa Shinto by removing Buddhist discourse from Yoshida Shinto and incorporating more Confucian teachings. Its ideology first posits that Shinto is the origin of all laws, and that [[Kuni-no-Tokotachi|Kunitokotachi]] (国常立尊) is the sovereign of the world. It argues that the world and humans were created through "{{ill|Li_(neo-Confucianism)|ja|理|lt=Li}}" (理), identical to the gods, and that "{{ill|Li_(neo-Confucianism)|ja|理|lt=Li}}" inherently exists within the human body. Thus, originally humans and gods were one, but the divine wisdom becomes clouded by the impurities of the human heart. Therefore, it is necessary to return to one's original state through "caution" (つつしみ). As concrete methods, it advocated purification rituals to cleanse both internally and externally, expressing sincerity through festival rites, and praying to the gods. Moreover, it stated that the five cardinal relationships in Confucianism are the mission given by the gods to humans, especially emphasizing the importance of the relationship between lord and retainer.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=522-528}}{{Cite web|date=2023-03-14|title=Yoshikawa Shintō {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230314175907/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9902|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}} == Meiji Restoration == In 1869 (Meiji 2), during the [[Meiji Restoration]] the traditional [[Japanese nobility]] were reformed. The Yoshida family were elevated to the kazoku peerage, and in 1884 (Meiji 17), upon the enactment of the {{ill|Peerage ordinance|ja|華族令}}, {{ill|Yoshida Yoshiyoshi|lt=Yoshiyoshi|ja|吉田良義}} was bestowed the title of [[viscount]]. The residence of the Yoshida baronial family was located in Ichigaya Nakanocho, Ushigome Ward, Tokyo. {{ill|Yoshida Kiyonari|en}} was another member who was also awarded the title of [[viscount]].{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PcG1AQAAQBAJ|title=The Satsuma Students in Britain: Japan's Early Search for the essence of the {{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}} (Yoshida)|image=File:Yoshida torii sakura 03.jpg|caption=Izumo Taisha, the traditional shrine of the family|parent house=[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]|image caption=[[Yoshida Shrine]], the traditional shrine of the family|alt=[[Yoshida Shrine]], the traditional shrine of the family}} The {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|en|draft:Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family}} ([[:ja:卜部氏|卜部氏]]) were a family of diviners in Japan{{Cite web |title=Yoshida family {{!}} Encyclopedia.com |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/yoshida-family |access-date=2023-03-12 |website=www.encyclopedia.com}}.{{rp|35}}. Their [[cadet branch]] the Yoshida family is one of the most historically influential shinto priest families. They were highly influential in the development of Shinto. The historical {{ill|Yoshida Shinto|en}} school of thought which was the norm until the [[Meiji Restoration]] is named after them.{{Cite web|date=2024-03-19|title=Yoshida Shintō {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151532/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9901|access-date=2024-03-19|website=web.archive.org}} They were originally the diviners of the Department of divinities under the Urabe clan name.{{Cite web|title=Jingidoke|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151308/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9910|access-date=2024-03-19|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} They served at [[Yoshida Shrine|Yoshida Shrine]], their traditional shrine and namesake.{{Cite web|title=Yoshida family|url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686?d=%2F10.1093%2Foi%2Fauthority.20110803125403686&p=emailAMFctfco71wyE|access-date=2024-03-19|website=Oxford Reference|language=en|doi=10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686?d=/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686&p=emailamfctfco71wye}} The Yoshida Family is a family of court nobles and kazoku descended from the Urabe Clan. As court nobles, they were classified as a {{ill|Half House|ja|半家 (公家)}}, and as {{ill|Kazoku|ja|華族}}, their rank was that of a [[viscount]]. == History == {{Main|en:History of Shinto}} The origins of the Yoshida family date back to the [[Heian period]] or earlier. They claimed descent from {{ill|Ame no Koyane|en}}.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_Q81DQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto: A History|last=Hardacre|first=Helen|date=2017|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-062171-1|language=en}}{{rp|25-26}} It is believed that originally the Urabe clan was a low clan subordinate to the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏|en||simple|User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan}}.{{Cite web|date=2024-03-19|title=Jingi shizoku {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151546/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9925|access-date=2024-04-01|website=web.archive.org}} They initially played support roles in rituals such as {{ill|Ōharae-shiki|en}}, but over time they expanded and managed to gain more power by monopolizing the role of ''miyaji'' until eventually becoming nearly in charge of the [[Department of Divinities]] as a whole. === Early history === In the {{ill|Department of Divinities|department of divinities|en}} there was this organization.{{rp|35}}.{{rp|25-26}} * The {{ill|Inbe clan|Inbe family|en||simple}} was responsible for managing the procuring materials for rituals and performing abstinence rites.{{rp|25-26}} and distribution of tribute offerings within the Jingikan..{{rp|35}} claiming descent from Ame no [[Futodama]] no Mikoto..{{rp|25-26}} * {{ill|Sarume clan|lt=Sarume family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|en:draft|6=ja|7=猿女君|8=fr|9=Clan Sarume}} women were tasked with performing sacred dances..{{rp|35}} Initially serving as seers and healers, their role evolved to include performing ritual dances, or kagura, during Enthronement Rites and court ceremonies..{{rp|25-26}} claiming descent from the goddess [[Ama-no-Uzume|Ame no Uzume]] no Mikoto..{{rp|25-26}} * The Tamatsukuri specialized in the creation of jewels..{{rp|35}} * The Kagamitsukuri were known for crafting {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=bronze mirrors|en}} for use in shrine ceremonies..{{rp|35}} * The {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|en|draft:Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family}} ([[:ja:卜部氏|卜部氏]]) considered to be of relatively low rank, carried out divination practices..{{rp|35}} using tortoise shells and deer scapulae {{rp|25-26}} later taking the surname {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Yoshida|ja|吉田家|en|draft:Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family}} and claiming descent from Ame no Koyane..{{rp|25-26}} * {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏|en||simple|User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan}}: Later known as the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|lt=Fujiwara|en}}, they specialized in reciting prayers to the Kami, with a divine lineage tracing back to {{ill|Ame no Koyane|en}} no Mikoto..{{rp|25-26}} ** In his book ''Jinja to kodai ōken saishi'' (1989). {{Interlanguage link multi|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup}} goes on to theorize that the {{Nihongo|{{ill|Ō clan|lt=Ō clan|ja|多氏}}|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}} was originally {{Nihongo|ōmi|大忌|"greater taboo (priesthood)"}}, but was usurped by the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏|en||simple|User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan}} who were among the "lesser priesthood" (the latter claims descent from the {{Nihongo|[[Inbe clan]]|[[:ja:忌部氏|忌部氏]]}}).{{cite book|title=神道の本|last=小向|first=正司|publisher=学研|year=1992|series=Books Esoterica|volume=2|pages=76–7}}(zasshi code 66951-07; kyōtsu zasshi code T10-66951-07-1000) ** Takemikazuchi was originally a local god (''kuni-tsu-kami'') revered by the {{Nihongo|{{ill|Ō clan|lt=Ō clan|ja|多氏}}|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}}, and was a god of maritime travel. However, the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏|en||simple|User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan}} who also has roots in this region, and when they took over control of priestly duties from the Ō clan, they also instituted Takemikazuchi as the Nakatomi clan's [[ujigami]] (clan deity). Or so this is the observation by {{Interlanguage link multi|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup}} {{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}} was the first person to have the name Yoshida, taken from [[Yoshida Shrine]] which he ran. The Yoshida faimly grew immensely powerful later. == Summary == Urabe is a clan whose occupation was Kameboku (divination by interpreting the cracks formed when a tortoise shell is burned). Different lineages of Urabe clans exist across Japan, with those from Izu (伊豆), Iki (壱岐), and Tsushima (対馬) appointed as officials of the Jingikan (神祇官). The Izu Urabe clan was appointed as vice-ministers (大副 and 少副) of the Jingikan, with 5 people from Izu, 5 from Iki, and 10 from Tsushima appointed to lower-ranking official positions, recognized for their excellence in divination techniques. It is said that Urabe clans not from these three regions are descendants of clans related to Taizan (太占), an ancient form of Japanese divination. == Urabe of Izu == - Surname: From Sukune Urabe (宿禰卜部) to Asaomi Urabe (朝臣卜部) - Ancestor: Hiramaro Urabe (平麻呂卜部) - Descendants include Kaneyoshi Urabe (兼好卜部) - The actual ancestor, Hiramaro Urabe, served in the early Heian period, but details before him are unclear. There are genealogies suggesting Hiramaro was the son of Onakatomi Chijimaro (大中臣千治麿), a grandson of Onakatomi Kiyomaro (大中臣清麿), but these are considered later fabrications. It is theorized they served Mishima Taisha Shrine (三嶋大社) as priests. The surname was changed from Sukune to Asaomi by Yoshida Kanehiro (吉田兼煕) in 1375. The descendants of Hiramaro split into the Yoshida-sha (吉田社) and Hirano-sha (平野社) lineages, serving alternately as Jingi Dai-Vice and Jingi Sho-Vice. == Urabe of Iki == The Iki Urabe clan, associated with Iyoshi Island (伊吉島). Genealogies indicate Maneko no Mikoto (真根子命), a descendant of Raijin no Mikoto (雷神命) and part of Empress Jingu's (神功皇后) retinue, as an ancestor. Despite some claims to Nakatomi (中臣) lineage, discrepancies in genealogical records suggest different origins.{{Cite journal|last=Kory|first=Stephan N.|date=2015|title=From Deer Bones to Turtle Shells: The State Ritualization of Pyro-Plastromancy during the Nara-Heian Transition|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/43686907|journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies|volume=42|issue=2|pages=339–380|issn=0304-1042}} == Urabe of Tsushima == The Tsushima Urabe clan, associated with the Tsushima Prefecture (対馬府) ruling family. Ancestral origins vary across historical sources, including deities like Takehiradori no Mikoto (建比良鳥命) and Raidaijin no Mikoto (雷大臣命).{{Cite journal|last=Grapard|first=Allan G.|date=1992|title=The Shinto of Yoshida Kanetomo|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2385357|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=47|issue=1|pages=27–58|doi=10.2307/2385357|issn=0027-0741}}{{Cite web|title=Cultural Properties {{!}} Japan Heritage Border Islands of Iki, Tsushima and Goto. A Bridge from Ancient Times.|url=https://kokkyonoshima.com/eng/places/bunkazai|access-date=2024-04-03|website=Cultural Properties {{!}} Japan Heritage Border Islands of Iki, Tsushima and Goto. A Bridge from Ancient Times.}}{{Cite web|title=Things to do in Tsushima in December|url=https://wanderlog.com/geoInMonth/506/12/tsushima-in-december|access-date=2024-04-03|website=Wanderlog}}{{Cite web|date=2024-03-19|title=Kiboku {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151536/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=8574|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}}https://web.archive.org/web/20240403160613/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9920 == Shrines served by the Urabe == - {{ill|Kashima-jingū|ja|鹿嶋神宮}} (鹿嶋神宮) in Hitachi Province: Served from ancient times, involved in divination. - {{ill|Katsuragi Hitotoshi Shrine|ja|葛城一言主神社}} (葛城一言主神社) in Yamato Province: Ancestor served as a priest. - {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社}} (宗像大社) in Chikuzen Province: Ancestors served, later becoming vassals of the {{ill|Kuroda clan|ja|黒田氏}} (黒田氏). == Other Urabe == Beyond the mentioned, the Urabe surname appears in ancient and Nara period records across regions like Mutsu (陸奥), Shimousa (下総), Suruga (駿河), Omi (近江), and Inaba (因幡) Provinces. == Yoshida family == The Yoshida Family is a family of court nobles and kazoku descended from the Urabe Clan. As court nobles, they were classified as a {{ill|Half House|ja|半家 (公家)}}, and as {{ill|Kazoku|ja|華族}}, their rank was that of a [[viscount]]. == Urabe Kanekata (fl. 1274 - 1301) == The Yoshida family (吉田家) originally bore the surname Urabe (卜部), and their lineage traditionally held the position of Jingi Daifu (神祇大副), the vice-official of the [[Department of Divinities]], specializing in divination by turtle shell throughout generations. In the medieval period, Urabe Kanekata (卜部兼方) was known for his expertise in Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) studies, earning the title "The Nihon Shoki Family."{{Cite web|date=2024-03-25|title=Urabe Kanekata {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240325211917/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9861|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}} == {{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}} (1348-1402) == The Yoshida family's founder, {{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}}, known for transferring his residence's land in Kyoto's Muromachi Koji to Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, named the family "Yoshida" after the [[Yoshida Shrine]], where he served. {{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|lt=Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}} was the first from the Urabe Clan to become a high-ranking official, serving as Jingi-no-Daifu (Deputy of the [[Department of Divinities]]) and Jiju (Chamberlain). == Yoshida Kanetomo (吉田 兼倶, 1435–1511) == The 5th generation, Kanetomo, founded a unique form of Shinto, expanding his influence by gaining Emperor Gomizunoo as a follower, despite fierce opposition from the existing priesthood of the Ise Shrine lineage. He self-proclaimed the new title of "Jingi Kanrei Chojou" (Supreme Leader of the Department of Worship), later ousting the Shirakawa family, who were Jingi Haku (heads of the Department of Worship), and expanding his control over shrines nationwide. [[File:吉田兼倶肖像画.jpg|thumb|Yoshida Kanetomo]] During the {{ill|Ōnin|en}} reign, the {{ill|Ōnin War|en}} broke out and Kyoto was burnt to the ground, affecting many temples and shrines, and causing the abortion of imperial court rituals such as the {{ill|Daijosai|en}} and the coronation ceremony. One of the priests who was shocked by the upheaval was {{ill|Yoshida Kanetomo|en}}. Kanetomo, who was so upset that he lost his own {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}} to the war, as well as more than a dozen residents of the area around the shrine.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=182}} However, the loss of many ancient manuscripts due to the war led to the formation of a new Shinto theory called {{ill|Yoshida Shintō|en}}.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=234}}[[File:Yoshida_shrine_funeral_hall.jpg|left|thumb|{{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en}} in {{ill|Sakyō-ku, Kyoto|lt=Sakyo-ku|en}} {{ill|Kyoto|Kyoto City|en}}]]Kanetomo authored texts such as "Shintō Daimi" (神道大意) and "Yuiitsu Shintō Meihō Yōshū" (唯一神道名法要集), synthesizing medieval Shinto thought and incorporating discourses from various religions to propose Yoshida Shinto. In this doctrine, he classified Shinto into three categories: "Honjaku Engi Shintō" (本迹縁起神道), "Ryōbu Shūgō Shintō" (両部習合神道), and "Genpon Shūgen Shintō" (元本宗源神道), declaring the "Genpon Shūgen Shintō" passed down in his family as the legitimate Shinto since the nation's founding. He defined gods as the "spiritual ancestors of heaven and earth" and the way as the "origin of all actions."{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=236-237}} He also strongly advocated the root-branch-fruit theory, positioning Shinto as the root, [[Confucianism]] as its branches manifesting in [[China]], and [[Buddhism]] as the fruit blossoming in India, asserting that Shinto encapsulates the essence of all religions.{{Sfn|Association of Shinto Shrines|2013|p=113}} Furthermore, Kanetomo argued that Shinto has three aspects: "substance" (体), "form" (相), and "function" (用), governing various phenomena like the sun and moon, cold and heat, and nature. Ultimately, he envisioned a pantheistic view where gods reside within all aspects of the universe, pervading the cosmos.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=237-238}} Kanetomo also established numerous rituals. He constructed the Dai Ōtomiya Saijō at the [[Yoshida Shrine]] precincts, proclaiming it as the foundation for rituals since Emperor Jimmu, serving as the main sanctuary for inner and outer shrines, eight god temples, and over three thousand official shrines nationwide.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=235-236}} Influenced by Esoteric Buddhism, he devised {{ill|Homa (ritual)|lt=Homa|en}} rituals involving a fire in an octagonal platform centered around a stove, contributing to the formation of three major rituals alongside "Jūhachido Shintō Gyoji" and "Sōgen Shintō Gyoji."{{Cite web|title=吉田神道行事壇|url=http://museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/exhibition/detail/id=4|access-date=2021-03-02|publisher=國學院大學博物館}} These teachings were expounded by the "Three Nerves" of the Tengen Shinhen Shinmyou Sutra, the Local Shinto Shinmyou Sutra, and the Jingen Shinryoku Shinmyou Sutra.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=236}} These sutras were said to be the teachings of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame-no-Koyane|en}}, but these three sutras are fictitious and there is no evidence that they were ever produced.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=239}} Kanetomo forged sutras similar to these by posing as the authors, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en}}, to create his own sutras.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|pp=239-240}} The history of the sanctuary was also created by Kanetomo himself.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=240}} Yoshida Shinto established the ritual of enshrining humans as gods. Traditionally, Shinto saw death as [[Kegare|impure]] and seldom involved in funeral rites, with human enshrinement limited to pacifying vengeful spirits or celestial deity worship. However, Yoshida Shinto, viewing a close relationship between humans and gods, actively conducted funerary rites, with Kanetomo establishing the Shinryūsha as a spiritual shrine over the deceased's remains.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=186-187}} Yoshida Shinto is the first Shinto theory to have its own doctrines, scriptures, and rituals independent of Buddhism, while integrating various religious discourses in a cross-border manner.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=243}}、The Shinto scholar {{ill|Okada Chuangji|ja|岡田莊司}} described the establishment of Yoshida Shinto as "a turning point in the history of Shinto.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=17}}、The historian {{ill|Toshio Kuroda|en}} argues that the establishment of Yoshida Shinto was the establishment of Shinto{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=16}} It is considered by several researchers to be a turning point in the history of Shinto. == Hino Tomiko (日野 富子, 1440 – June 30, 1496) == Although Yoshida Shinto was an emerging force, it rapidly rose to prominence, perhaps due to the social unrest of the age of war, and was widely accepted, especially by the upper classes, as it received the support of {{ill|Hino Tomiko|en}} in the construction of the Omoto Shrine, and even received the imperial approval of the Omoto Shrine in {{ill|1473|en}} ({{ill|Bunmei|en}}5).{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=235}}、The center of the Shinto world in modern times.{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=244}} On the other hand, it received strong protests from priests of [[Ise Grand Shrine]].{{Sfn|Satoshi Ito|2012|p=243}} == {{ill|Yoshida Kanemi|ja|吉田兼見|fa|یوشیدا کانه‌می}} (1535-1610) == As mentioned above, Yoshida Shinto, which established Shinto funeral rites, became involved in the construction of shrines that enshrined warring feudal lords as gods in the Warring States period, and Kanemi Yoshida was involved in the construction of {{ill|Toyokuni Shrine (Kyoto)|lt=Toyokuni Shrine|en}}, which enshrined {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en}} as a god. Shinryuin Bonshun of the Yoshida family taught Shinto to {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en}}, and according to his will, conducted a Shinto funeral service after Ieyasu's death.{{Cite web|last=鎌田純一|date=2017-10-19|title=梵舜|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%A2%B5%E8%88%9C-135079|access-date=2021-07-06|publisher=コトバンク（日本大百科全書）}}(However, {{ill|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|en}} became the {{ill|Sanno Shinto|en}} style after {{ill|Tenkai|en}} won the debate). When the era of warfare ended and the Edo period began, the administration of shrines was reorganized. The shogunate first relieved each shrine of its current territory and granted it the privilege of "not entering into the custody of the guardian. However, what was granted was the right to make profits from the shrines, and the ownership of the land belonged to the shogunate.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=191}} The {{ill|Shogun|lt=Shogunate|en}} also established the {{ill|Jisha-bugyō|en}} as a position reporting directly to the shogun, and placed it at the head of the three magistrates, surpassing the {{ill|Machi-bugyō|lt=Town Magistrate|en}} and {{ill|Kanjō-bugyō|lt=Account Magistrate|en}} under the jurisdiction of the {{ill|Rōjū|lt=Rōchū|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=191-192}} In addition, a Shinto department under the jurisdiction of the temple and shrine magistrates was established to study the truths of Shinto and the rituals of rituals and to respond to the advice of the temple and shrine magistrates.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=192}} On the other hand, individual magistrates were assigned to specific shrines, such as {{ill|Yamada bugyō|en}}, who was in charge of Ise Shrine, and Nikko bugyō, who was in charge of {{ill|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|lt=Nikko Tōshō-gū|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=198}} By the 9th generation, {{ill|Yoshida Kanemi|ja|吉田兼見|fa|یوشیدا کانه‌می}}, with the support of [[Oda Nobunaga]], the family achieved the court noble status{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Yoshida Kanemi {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207101954/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9845|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}}. Serving as a family ritualist to Konoe Sakihisa and forming a deep friendship with Akechi Mitsuhide, Kanemi's diary, "Kanjokyoki," became an essential resource for the study of the Azuchi-Momoyama period. The Yoshida family's dominance in priesthood was solidified in the [[Edo period]], particularly with the "Various Shrine's Negi and Kannushi Laws" in 1665. In {{ill|1665|en}} (the fifth year of the {{ill|Kanbun (era)|lt=Kanbun|en}}), the shogunate issued the Priest Law for Priests of Various Shrines, which stated that ordinary {{ill|Kannushi|lt=Priests|en}} without rank must obtain a Shinto license issued by the Yoshida family before they can wear a hunting robe or crown, giving the Yoshida family control over almost all priests.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=192-196}} However, it was approved that those families that had been conferred ranks by the Imperial Court through transmission, such as [[Ise Grand Shrine]], {{ill|Kamo Shrine|en}}, {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}, {{ill|Usa Jingū|en}}, {{ill|Izumo-taisha|en}}, and {{ill|Fushimi Inari-taisha|en}}, would continue to use the same methods as before, without the Yoshida family.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|p=193}} In addition, the law stipulates penalties for neglect of duties by priests, prohibition of sales and purchases of shrine property, and the obligation to repair shrine buildings. The Shogunate also financially supported the partial revival of the imperial rituals that had been suspended due to warfare. After 222 years of interruptions since {{ill|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|en}}, the Dai-namesai was revived in the reign of {{ill|Emperor Higashiyama|en}}, and became a regular event since {{ill|Emperor Sakuramachi|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} The {{ill|Niiname-no-Matsuri|en}} was also revived in {{ill|1688|en}} (the first year of {{ill|Genroku|en}}), the year after the restoration of the Dai-namesai.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} In {{ill|1744|en}} (the first year of {{ill|Enkyō (Edo period)|Enkyo|en}}), some of the votive offerings were also revived, including those to {{ill|Twenty-Two Shrines|en}} and to Usa Hachiman Shrine and {{ill|Kashii-gū|lt=Kashii Shrine|en}}.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=188-190}} The Imperial Court's dispatch of imperial envoys on the occasion of the Shinnamesai festival was revived in {{ill|1647|en}} (the fourth year of the {{ill|Shōhō|lt=Shohoho|en}}) by the special order of {{ill|Emperor Go-Kōmyō|en}}. The ceremonial relocation of the Ise Jingu Shrine was also suspended, but was rebuilt during the {{ill|Azuchi-Momoyama period|lt2=Orifuji administration|en}} thanks to the efforts of Seisun and Shuyou of Keikoin. The {{ill|Department of Divinities|en}}, which was destroyed by fire during the war, was replaced by the eight temples at the Yoshida Shrine, and the Divinities themselves were not rebuilt.{{Sfn|Shouji Okada|2010|pp=190-191}} == Later Edo period == The family heads were known as Jingi Kanrei Chojou, holding the highest position of Jingi-no-Daifu at the rank of Shonii (Senior Second Rank). During the Edo period, the family's stipend was 760 koku. A branch family, the Hagiwara family, emerged in the early Edo period. In Yoshida Shinto, a merchant named {{ill|Yoshikawa Tadashi|ja|吉川惟足}} was initiated into the Yoshida family and received the "Shinto Doutou" (神道同統) from the head of the Yoshida family, Hagiwara Kenju (萩原兼従), becoming the official successor. He formed Yoshikawa Shinto by removing Buddhist discourse from Yoshida Shinto and incorporating more Confucian teachings. Its ideology first posits that Shinto is the origin of all laws, and that [[Kuni-no-Tokotachi|Kunitokotachi]] (国常立尊) is the sovereign of the world. It argues that the world and humans were created through "{{ill|Li_(neo-Confucianism)|ja|理|lt=Li}}" (理), identical to the gods, and that "{{ill|Li_(neo-Confucianism)|ja|理|lt=Li}}" inherently exists within the human body. Thus, originally humans and gods were one, but the divine wisdom becomes clouded by the impurities of the human heart. Therefore, it is necessary to return to one's original state through "caution" (つつしみ). As concrete methods, it advocated purification rituals to cleanse both internally and externally, expressing sincerity through festival rites, and praying to the gods. Moreover, it stated that the five cardinal relationships in Confucianism are the mission given by the gods to humans, especially emphasizing the importance of the relationship between lord and retainer.{{Sfn|Taira Shigemichi|Akie Abe|1972|pp=522-528}}{{Cite web|date=2023-03-14|title=Yoshikawa Shintō {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230314175907/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9902|access-date=2024-04-03|website=web.archive.org}} == Meiji Restoration == In 1869 (Meiji 2), during the [[Meiji Restoration]] the traditional [[Japanese nobility]] were reformed. The Yoshida family were elevated to the kazoku peerage, and in 1884 (Meiji 17), upon the enactment of the {{ill|Peerage ordinance|ja|華族令}}, {{ill|Yoshida Yoshiyoshi|lt=Yoshiyoshi|ja|吉田良義}} was bestowed the title of [[viscount]]. The residence of the Yoshida baronial family was located in Ichigaya Nakanocho, Ushigome Ward, Tokyo. {{ill|Yoshida Kiyonari|en}} was another member who was also awarded the title of [[viscount]].{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PcG1AQAAQBAJ|title=The Satsuma Students in Britain: Japan's Early Search for the essence of the {{Draft}}{{Promising draft}} {{Expand Japanese}} [[en:draft:Yoshida family]] [[ja:卜部氏]] {{Infobox Japanese clan|province of origin=[[Yamashiro Province]]|home province=[[Yamashiro Province]]|founder={{ill|Ame no Koyane|en}} (Urabe)
{{ill|Yoshida Kanehiro|ja|吉田兼煕}} (Yoshida)|image=File:Yoshida torii sakura 03.jpg|caption=Izumo Taisha, the traditional shrine of the family|parent house=[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]|image caption=[[Yoshida Shrine]], the traditional shrine of the family|alt=[[Yoshida Shrine]], the traditional shrine of the family}} The {{Interlanguage link|Yoshida family|lt=Urabe clan|ja|卜部氏|en|draft:Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Urabe_clan|fr|User:Immanuelle/Urabe_clan}} ([[:ja:卜部氏|卜部氏]]) were a family of diviners in Japan{{Cite web |title=Yoshida family {{!}} Encyclopedia.com |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/yoshida-family |access-date=2023-03-12 |website=www.encyclopedia.com}}.{{rp|35}}. Their [[cadet branch]] the Yoshida family is one of the most historically influential shinto priest families. They were highly influential in the development of Shinto. The historical {{ill|Yoshida Shinto|en}} school of thought which was the norm until the [[Meiji Restoration]] is named after them.{{Cite web|date=2024-03-19|title=Yoshida Shintō {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151532/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9901|access-date=2024-03-19|website=web.archive.org}} They were originally the diviners of the Department of divinities under the Urabe clan name.{{Cite web|title=Jingidoke|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151308/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9910|access-date=2024-03-19|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} They served at [[Yoshida Shrine|Yoshida Shrine]], their traditional shrine and namesake.{{Cite web|title=Yoshida family|url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686?d=%2F10.1093%2Foi%2Fauthority.20110803125403686&p=emailAMFctfco71wyE|access-date=2024-03-19|website=Oxford Reference|language=en|doi=10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686?d=/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803125403686&p=emailamfctfco71wye}} The Yoshida Family is a family of court nobles and kazoku descended from the Urabe Clan. As court nobles, they were classified as a {{ill|Half House|ja|半家 (公家)}}, and as {{ill|Kazoku|ja|華族}}, their rank was that of a [[viscount]]. == History == {{Main|en:History of Shinto}} The origins of the Yoshida family date back to the [[Heian period]] or earlier. They claimed descent from {{ill|Ame no Koyane|en}}.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_Q81DQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto: A History|last=Hardacre|first=Helen|date=2017|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-062171-1|language=en}}{{rp|25-26}} It is believed that originally the Urabe clan was a low clan subordinate to the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏|en||simple|User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan}}.{{Cite web|date=2024-03-19|title=Jingi shizoku {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319151546/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9925|access-date=2024-04-01|website=web.archive.org}} They initially played support roles in rituals such as {{ill|Ōharae-shiki|en}}, but over time they expanded and managed to gain more power by monopolizing the role of ''miyaji'' until eventually becoming nearly in charge of the [[Department of Divinities]] as a whole. === Early history === In the {{ill|Department of Divinities|department of divinities|en}} there was this organization.{{rp|35}}.{{rp|25-26}} * The {{ill|Inbe clan|Inbe family|en||simple}} was responsible for managing the procuring materials for rituals and performing abstinence rites.{{rp|25-26}} and distribution of tribute offerings within the Jingikan..{{rp|35}} claiming descent from Ame no [[Futodama]] no Mikoto..{{rp|25-26}} * {{ill|Sarume clan|lt=Sarume family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|en:draft|6=ja|7=猿女君|8=fr|9=Clan Sarume}} women were tasked with performing sacred dances..{{rp|35}} Initially serving as seers and healers, their role evolved to include performing ritual dances, or kagura, during Enthronement Rites and
